lessons.title: What Is a Compiler?
lessons.content:
Imagine your grandmother in Sylhet wants to send a long letter to a cousin in Japan who only reads Japanese. She hires a translator. The translator reads the whole letter, understands what grandmother means, writes a full Japanese version, checks it for mistakes and hands it over. The cousin never sees the Bangla letter at all; he only reads the translation. A compiler is exactly that translator, but for programs. You write in a language people find comfortable, like C or Java, and the compiler produces a version in the language the machine actually understands.

What it is: A compiler is a program that reads a whole program written in one language, called the source language, and translates it into an equivalent program in another language, called the target language. Usually the source is a high-level language such as C, C++, Rust or Go, and the target is machine code or assembly for a real processor. The word equivalent is important: the translated program must do exactly what the original program says, nothing more and nothing less. A second job of every compiler is to report errors in the source program, such as a missing semicolon or adding a number to a string where the language forbids it.

The problem it solves: A processor understands only machine code, patterns of bytes like B8 07 00. In the Microprocessors course you saw how painful it is to write even a loop in assembly: you must choose registers, remember which flag a jump checks and manage the stack by hand. A big program like a banking app or a web browser has millions of lines. Writing all of that in assembly would take forever, would be full of bugs and would only run on one processor family. People needed a way to write programs in a language close to human thinking, like total = price * quantity, and have a machine do the boring, error-prone translation.

Before compilers: In the late 1940s and early 1950s, programmers wrote machine code or assembly by hand. Many experts believed a program that writes programs could never produce code as fast as a skilled human. Grace Hopper built a system called A-0 around 1952 that turned a kind of shorthand into machine code, and it is often called one of the first compilers. The real turning point was FORTRAN, released by an IBM team led by John Backus in 1957. Its compiler produced code good enough that scientists accepted it, and it showed that high-level languages were practical. Almost every language since has followed that path.

Compiler vs interpreter: An interpreter also runs high-level programs, but it does not produce a separate target program first. It reads the source (or some internal form of it) and carries out each statement directly, one after another, while the program runs. A compiler translates first and runs later. Think of the difference between a translator who writes a full Japanese book (compiler) and a live interpreter standing next to a speaker who translates each sentence as it is spoken (interpreter). The translated book can be read again and again without the translator; the live interpreter is needed every time.

Trade-offs between the two: Compiled programs usually run faster, because the translation work is done once, before running, and the compiler has time to improve the code. Interpreters usually give better error messages at the exact line where something goes wrong, and you can change a line and run again immediately. A compiled C program for Windows on an x86 laptop will not run on an ARM phone; you must compile again for that target. An interpreted Python script runs anywhere a Python interpreter exists.

Hybrid systems: Many real languages mix both ideas. Java source code is compiled by javac into bytecode, a compact machine-independent instruction set. The Java Virtual Machine then runs that bytecode, partly by interpreting it and partly by compiling hot parts into real machine code while the program is running. That last trick is called just-in-time (JIT) compilation. Python also compiles source to bytecode (the .pyc files you may have seen) and then interprets the bytecode. JavaScript engines in Chrome and Firefox use JIT compilers too. So the line between compiler and interpreter is not a wall; it is a design choice.

Other translators: An assembler translates assembly language into machine code; it is a simple compiler where each line usually becomes one instruction. A preprocessor, like the C preprocessor, handles #include and #define before real compilation starts. A source-to-source translator, sometimes called a transpiler, converts one high-level language into another, for example TypeScript into JavaScript. A decompiler tries to go backwards, from machine code to something like source. All of these share techniques you will learn in this course.

Why study compilers: Very few of you will write a full C compiler for a job. But the ideas show up everywhere. Every time a program reads structured text it needs lexing and parsing: JSON and XML readers, SQL engines in databases, spreadsheet formula bars, configuration files, template engines and even calculator apps. Code editors like VS Code use parsers to colour your code and find errors as you type. Knowing how compilers optimize makes you write faster code and read error messages calmly. And the course ties together everything you learned: automata, grammars, data structures, algorithms, assembly and computer architecture.

What makes a good compiler: First and most important, correctness: the target program must mean the same as the source. A fast compiler that sometimes changes the meaning is useless and dangerous. Next, good error messages that point to the right line and explain the problem. Then the quality of the output code: fast to run, small in size, low in energy use on phones. Then the speed of compiling itself, because developers compile many times a day. Finally, the compiler should be maintainable, since languages and processors keep changing.

A first look inside: A compiler does not translate in one jump. It works in stages, like a factory line. First it reads characters and groups them into words called tokens. Then it checks that the tokens form valid sentences according to the grammar of the language and builds a tree. Then it checks meaning, such as types. Then it produces an intermediate form that is easy to work with, improves it, and finally produces target code. We will trace a single statement through all these stages in the next lesson.

Where theory meets practice: In Theory of Computation you met regular expressions, finite automata and context-free grammars as abstract ideas. In this course they become tools. Regular expressions describe tokens, and finite automata become the lexer. Context-free grammars describe the syntax of the language, and pushdown-style parsers check it. You will not need to re-prove theorems here; you will build tables and run them on real input.

A tiny example of translation: Take the C statement x = a + b * 2. A compiler for an x86-style machine might produce something like: load b into a register, multiply it by 2, add a to it, store the result into x. Notice that the compiler had to know that * happens before +, which came from the grammar. It had to know where a, b and x live in memory, which came from the symbol table. And it may have replaced multiply by 2 with a cheaper shift or add, which is an optimization.

Real life example 1, a Bangladeshi software company: A team in Dhaka builds a payment backend in Go. Each time a developer pushes code, the build server runs the Go compiler. In a few seconds it checks every file for type errors, rejects code that uses a variable that was never declared and produces one fast executable for Linux servers. If someone writes amount := '100' + 5 by mistake, the compiler stops the build with a type error before the code ever reaches a real customer's money. The compiler is acting like a strict quality checker at the factory gate.

Real life example 2, a phone app on a cheap Android phone: Many people in Bangladesh use low-cost Android phones. Android apps written in Kotlin or Java are compiled into bytecode, and on the phone the Android runtime compiles that bytecode further into native ARM machine code, partly ahead of time and partly using profiles of how the app is used. That is why an app can feel faster after a few days of use. Good compiler work directly saves battery and time for millions of users.

Compile time vs run time: Two words will appear in every lesson, so fix them now. Compile time is when the compiler is working on your source code, before the program runs. Run time is when the translated program is actually executing on the machine with real input. Some facts are known at compile time, such as the type of a variable declared as int, or the value of 3 * 4 written directly in the code. Other facts are only known at run time, such as the number a user types in or how many items are in a shopping cart. A big part of compiler design is moving as much work and as many checks as possible to compile time, because work done once at compile time is free at every run. An error caught at compile time is caught on the developer's laptop; an error caught at run time may be caught in front of a customer.

Course map: Lessons 2 to 5 cover the overall structure and the lexical analyzer: tokens, regular definitions and turning regular expressions into a fast DFA-based lexer, plus Lex. Lessons 6 to 14 cover parsing: grammars, top-down parsing with FIRST, FOLLOW and LL(1) tables, and bottom-up parsing with SLR, canonical LR and LALR tables and the Yacc tool. Lessons 15 to 17 add meaning: syntax-directed translation and type checking. Lessons 18 to 20 produce intermediate code. Lesson 21 explains what happens at run time: stacks, activation records and parameter passing. Lessons 22 to 25 cover code generation, register allocation and optimization.

Common mistakes: Some students think a compiler runs the program; it does not, it only translates and checks. Others think interpreters never compile anything; many interpreters compile to bytecode first. Many believe compiled code is always faster than interpreted code; usually true, but a JIT can sometimes beat a simple compiler. Some confuse the compiler with the IDE or editor; the editor is just where you type. Finally, a compiler that finds no errors does not mean the program is correct; it only means the program follows the language rules.

What exams ask: Define a compiler and an interpreter and compare them with advantages and disadvantages. Explain why compilers are needed. List the main phases of a compiler. Explain hybrid compilation in Java. Name and describe other language processors such as assembler, preprocessor, linker and loader. Short notes on JIT compilation and cross compilers are common too.

Recap: A compiler translates a whole source program into an equivalent target program and reports errors. It exists because humans cannot productively write large programs in machine code. Interpreters execute directly instead of producing a target program, and modern systems often mix both with bytecode and JIT. Correctness comes first, then good errors, fast output and fast compiling. Next lesson we open the factory and walk one statement through every phase.
key_points: A compiler translates a whole source program into an equivalent target program and reports errors in the source.
An interpreter executes the program directly without producing a separate target program.
Compiled code usually runs faster; interpreters give quicker edit-run cycles and run anywhere the interpreter exists.
Java and Python compile to bytecode first; JIT compilers turn hot bytecode into machine code at run time.
FORTRAN (1957, John Backus's team at IBM) proved compiled high-level languages were practical.
Correctness is the first requirement of a compiler, then good error messages, fast output code and fast compiling.
Compiler techniques (lexing, parsing) appear in JSON readers, SQL engines, editors and formula bars.
lessons.tip: Keep one small statement, like x = a + b * 2, in your head for the whole course. For every new topic ask: what does this phase do to my little statement?

lessons.title: The Structure of a Compiler
lessons.content:
Think of a garment factory in Gazipur. Raw cloth comes in at one door. One team cuts it into pieces, another team checks the pieces against the pattern, another sews them together, another checks the quality, another irons and folds, and finally a team packs shirts into boxes for shipping. No single worker does everything, and each team trusts that the team before it did its job. A compiler is organised the same way: a line of phases, each taking the output of the previous one, each doing one clear job.

Two big halves: Every compiler has an analysis part and a synthesis part. Analysis reads the source program, breaks it into pieces, checks it against the rules of the language and builds an internal picture of what the program means. Synthesis takes that internal picture and builds the target program. The analysis part is usually called the front end and the synthesis part the back end. Between them sits an intermediate representation, a middle language that both halves understand.

The six classic phases: Textbooks usually list six phases: lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, code optimization and code generation. Two helpers work beside all of them: the symbol table manager and the error handler. We will now trace one statement through every phase, because seeing it once makes the whole course easier. The statement is position = initial + rate * 60, where position, initial and rate are floating-point variables.

Phase 1, lexical analysis: The lexer, also called the scanner, reads the raw characters p, o, s, i, t, i, o, n, space, =, and so on. It groups them into meaningful units called lexemes and outputs a token for each one. For our statement it produces: <id,1> <=> <id,2> <+> <id,3> <*> <60>. Here id is the token name for identifiers, and the number after it is a pointer to that name's entry in the symbol table, where entry 1 is position, entry 2 is initial and entry 3 is rate. Spaces are thrown away. The lexer turned 30 characters into 7 tokens.

Phase 2, syntax analysis: The parser takes the token stream and checks that it follows the grammar of the language. It builds a tree that shows the structure. The root is the assignment =. Its left child is id1 (position). Its right child is a + node whose left child is id2 (initial) and whose right child is a * node with children id3 (rate) and 60. Notice that the tree already encodes precedence: * sits lower than +, so it will be computed first. If the programmer had written position = initial + * rate, the parser would report a syntax error here.

Phase 3, semantic analysis: Now the compiler checks meaning, using the tree and the symbol table. The most important check is type checking. Are all names declared? Are the operands of * compatible? Here rate is a float but 60 is an integer. The language allows mixing them, so the semantic analyzer inserts a conversion node, inttofloat(60), into the tree. If rate had been a string, this is where an error such as invalid operands to * would appear. Syntax is about form; semantics is about meaning.

Phase 4, intermediate code generation: The compiler now walks the checked tree and produces a simple, machine-like intermediate code. A popular form is three-address code, where each instruction has at most one operator on the right side. Our statement becomes: t1 = inttofloat(60); t2 = id3 * t1; t3 = id2 + t2; id1 = t3. The names t1, t2, t3 are temporaries the compiler invented. This code is easy to generate, easy to analyse and easy to translate to many different machines.

Phase 5, code optimization: The optimizer tries to make the intermediate code better without changing its meaning. Better usually means faster, but it can also mean smaller or using less energy. Here it notices that inttofloat(60) can be done right now, at compile time, giving 60.0, so t1 disappears. It also notices that t3 is only used to copy into id1, so the copy can go. The result is two instructions: t1 = id3 * 60.0; id1 = id2 + t1. Real optimizers do much more, as you will see in lessons 23 to 25.

Phase 6, code generation: Finally the code generator maps intermediate code to real target instructions, choosing registers and memory locations. For a simple register machine it might produce: LDF R2, id3 (load rate into register R2); MULF R2, R2, #60.0 (multiply by the constant 60.0); LDF R1, id2 (load initial); ADDF R1, R1, R2 (add); STF id1, R1 (store into position). The F means floating point and # marks an immediate constant. Deciding which values live in which registers is one of the hardest parts of this phase.

The symbol table: The symbol table is a data structure, usually a hash table, with one record per name in the program. A record holds the name, its type, where it is stored, its scope and, for functions, the number and types of parameters and the return type. The lexer or parser inserts names; the semantic analyzer reads types from it; the code generator reads addresses from it. Because every phase looks names up many times, the table must allow fast insert and fast lookup.

The error handler: Each phase can find errors. The lexer finds illegal characters such as @ in a C identifier. The parser finds syntax errors such as a missing closing bracket. The semantic analyzer finds type errors and undeclared variables. A good compiler does not stop at the first error. It reports it, recovers somehow and continues, so the programmer sees many errors in one compile. Lessons 6, 9 and 14 show how parsers recover.

Phases vs passes: A phase is a logical step. A pass is one reading of the whole program, from start to end, which may include several phases. Early compilers used many passes because memory was tiny. Modern compilers often group the front-end phases into one pass that produces intermediate code, then run several optimization passes over that code, then one code generation pass. A one-pass compiler is simple and fast but cannot easily use information that appears later in the file, such as a function defined after it is called.

Why split front end and back end: Suppose you want compilers for 5 languages on 4 machines. Without a shared middle you need 5 x 4 = 20 full compilers. With a common intermediate representation you need 5 front ends and 4 back ends, just 9 pieces. This is exactly how GCC and LLVM are organised: Clang is a front end for C and C++, Rust and Swift also have front ends that produce LLVM IR, and LLVM has back ends for x86, ARM, RISC-V and others.

The cousins of the compiler: Writing gcc main.c and getting a running program involves more than the compiler. The preprocessor expands #include files and #define macros and removes comments. The compiler produces assembly. The assembler turns assembly into relocatable machine code, an object file, where addresses are not final yet. The linker joins several object files and library code into one executable and fixes the addresses, for example where printf really lives. Finally, the loader, part of the operating system, copies the executable into memory and starts it.

Compiler construction tools: Because some phases follow fixed recipes, tools can generate them. Scanner generators like Lex and Flex build a lexer from regular expressions. Parser generators like Yacc and Bison build an LR parser from a grammar. Syntax-directed translation engines, code generator generators and data-flow analysis frameworks help with later phases. LLVM itself is used as a toolkit by many new languages so that they do not have to write a back end from scratch.

Bootstrapping and T-diagrams: A compiler is itself a program, so it must be written in some language. A compiler is described by three languages: source S, target T and implementation language I. A T-diagram draws this as a T shape with S on the left arm, T on the right arm and I at the bottom. Bootstrapping means writing a compiler for language L in L itself. You first write a tiny compiler for a small subset of L in some existing language, use it to compile a better compiler written in that subset, and repeat. Modern C compilers and the Go compiler are written in their own languages.

Cross compilers: A cross compiler runs on one machine but produces code for another. A developer in Dhaka writing firmware for an ARM microcontroller in a smart electricity meter compiles on an x86 laptop, but the output must run on the ARM chip. In T-diagram terms, the implementation runs on x86 while the target is ARM. Android and iPhone app builds also use cross compilation.

Real life example 1, a spelling and grammar checker: When you type a Bangla sentence in a word processor, a similar pipeline runs. First the text is split into words (like lexing), then grammar rules are checked (like parsing), then meaning issues may be flagged (like semantic checks). The idea of phases, each doing one job and passing its output on, is the same.

Real life example 2, a university result processing system: A university office receives marks as a long CSV file. A small program reads characters and splits them into fields (lexing), checks every row has roll, course code and marks in the right order (parsing), checks that marks are between 0 and 100 and roll numbers exist (semantic checks), converts marks into grade points (translation), and finally prints transcripts (code generation). If a row is broken, it reports the line and continues with the next row, just like compiler error recovery.

Common mistakes: Students often mix up syntax errors and semantic errors. A missing semicolon is syntax; using an undeclared variable or adding an int array to a float is semantic. Another mistake is to think the optimizer is required; a compiler can skip it and still be correct. Some forget that tokens carry attributes, such as the symbol table pointer for identifiers. Many also think the linker is part of the compiler; it is a separate program.

What exams ask: Draw the phases of a compiler and show the output of each phase for position = initial + rate * 60, or a similar statement. Explain the role of the symbol table and error handler. Differentiate phase and pass, front end and back end. Explain the language processing system with preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker and loader. Explain bootstrapping and cross compilers with T-diagrams.

Recap: A compiler is a pipeline: lexical analysis makes tokens, syntax analysis makes a tree, semantic analysis checks meaning and types, intermediate code generation makes three-address code, optimization improves it and code generation makes target instructions. The symbol table and error handler serve all phases. Splitting into front end and back end around a common intermediate form saves effort. Next lesson we zoom into phase 1, the lexical analyzer.
key_points: Analysis (front end) understands the source; synthesis (back end) builds the target; an intermediate representation connects them.
Six phases: lexical, syntax, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, optimization, code generation.
position = initial + rate * 60 becomes tokens, then a tree, then a tree with inttofloat, then three-address code, then optimized code, then machine instructions.
The symbol table stores each name's type, scope and location and is used by every phase.
A phase is a logical step; a pass is one full read of the program and may contain several phases.
Preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker and loader together turn source into a running program.
Bootstrapping writes a compiler in its own language; a cross compiler runs on one machine and targets another.
lessons.tip: Memorise the full trace of position = initial + rate * 60 through all six phases. It is the single most common long question in compiler exams.

lessons.title: Lexical Analysis: Tokens, Lexemes and Patterns
lessons.content:
Imagine a teacher in a village school reading a page of Bangla handwriting from a student who forgot to put spaces between words. Before she can check grammar, she has to find where each word starts and ends, and decide what kind of word it is: a name, a number, a verb. Only then can she check whether the sentence makes sense. The first phase of a compiler has this exact job. It reads a long stream of characters and cuts it into words, so that the next phase can work with words instead of single letters.

What it is: The lexical analyzer, also called the lexer or scanner, is the first phase of the compiler. Its input is the source program as a sequence of characters. Its output is a sequence of tokens. Along the way it removes things the parser does not care about, such as spaces, tabs, newlines and comments, and it keeps track of line numbers so that error messages can say error on line 42. It also usually enters identifiers into the symbol table.

How it talks to the parser: In most compilers the lexer does not produce the whole token list at once. Instead, the parser calls a function, often named getNextToken, whenever it needs the next token. The lexer reads just enough characters to form one token and returns it. This keeps memory use small and lets the two phases work together like a hand passing bricks to a mason one at a time.

Why a separate phase: You could, in theory, let the parser read characters directly. Compilers separate the lexer for three reasons. First, simplicity: the grammar for the parser becomes much smaller if it does not have to describe spaces, comments and the spelling of every number. Second, efficiency: the lexer touches every single character of the program, so it is worth making it very fast with special techniques such as buffering and DFA tables. Third, portability: odd details of the input, such as character encodings or special symbols on some keyboards, can be handled in the lexer alone.

Token, lexeme and pattern: These three words are the vocabulary of this lesson, so learn them carefully. A token is a pair of a token name and an optional attribute value. The token name is an abstract category, such as id, number, relop or the keyword if. A lexeme is the actual sequence of characters in the source that matches a token, such as count, 3.14 or >=. A pattern is the rule that describes which lexemes belong to a token, such as a letter followed by letters or digits for identifiers. One token name can have many lexemes: count, total and x1 are all lexemes of the token id.

A small table in words: For the token if, the pattern is the exact characters i then f, and the only lexeme is if. For relop, the pattern is one of <, <=, =, <>, >, >= in some languages, or <, <=, ==, !=, >, >= in C, and the lexemes are those symbols. For id, the pattern is a letter followed by letters and digits, and lexemes include pi, score and D2. For number, the pattern is any numeric constant, with lexemes like 3.14159, 0 and 6.02e23. For literal, the pattern is anything between double quotes except a double quote, as in a C string.

Attributes: When several lexemes share a token name, the parser only needs the name, but later phases need to know which lexeme it was. So the lexer attaches an attribute. For an identifier, the attribute is usually a pointer to its symbol table entry, which stores the lexeme, its type and its location. For a number, the attribute might be the numeric value itself or a pointer to a constant table. For relop, the attribute says which operator it is, such as LT or GE. Keywords and punctuation usually need no attribute.

Worked example: Take the C line: if (count >= 10) total = total + 1; The lexer produces, in order: <if>, <(>, <id, pointer to count>, <relop, GE>, <number, 10>, <)>, <id, pointer to total>, <=>, <id, pointer to total>, <+>, <number, 1>, <;>. That is 12 tokens. Notice the two total lexemes give the same symbol table pointer, because they are the same name. Notice also that = here is the assignment token, not a relop, because in C comparison for equality is ==.

What the lexer removes: White space separates tokens but is not itself a token in most languages, so the lexer skips it. Comments are also skipped; for C that means everything between /* and */ and everything after // until the end of the line. Python is a famous exception: there indentation matters, so the Python lexer turns changes in indentation into special INDENT and DEDENT tokens that the parser uses like opening and closing braces.

Lookahead: Often the lexer cannot decide a token from one character. When it sees >, it does not know yet whether the token is > or >=. It must read the next character. If that is =, the token is >=. If it is anything else, the token is > and the extra character must be pushed back, a step called retracting, so it can start the next token. Reading ahead one or two characters is normal and cheap.

A famous hard case: Old FORTRAN ignored blanks completely. The statement DO 5 I = 1.25 means assign 1.25 to a variable called DO5I, because there is a dot. The statement DO 5 I = 1,25 means a loop from 1 to 25 ending at label 5, because there is a comma. The lexer cannot tell which until it reaches the dot or comma far ahead. Modern languages avoid this by making spaces significant and reserving keywords, which is why language designers think about the lexer when they design a language.

Input buffering, the problem: Reading the source file one character at a time with a system call is very slow, because each call to the operating system has overhead. Also, because of lookahead, the lexer sometimes needs to look at characters beyond the end of the current lexeme and then go back. So we need a smart way to read large chunks into memory and still move freely within them.

Buffer pairs: The classic solution uses two buffers, each of size N characters, where N is typically the size of a disk block such as 4096. One read command fills a whole buffer at once. Two pointers move over the buffers: lexemeBegin marks the start of the current lexeme, and forward scans ahead until a pattern match is found. When forward reaches the end of one buffer, the other buffer is refilled with the next N characters and forward moves into it. Because there are two halves, a lexeme that crosses the boundary still sits in memory. The only limit is that a single lexeme plus lookahead cannot be longer than N.

Sentinels: With plain buffer pairs, each time forward moves, the code must make two tests: did we reach the end of the buffer, and what character is this? Since this happens for every character of the program, it adds up. The trick is to put a special sentinel character, usually called eof, at the end of each buffer. Now the loop makes only one test per character: is it eof? Only when the answer is yes do we check whether it is the end of a buffer (then reload the other one) or the true end of the input (then stop). One test instead of two, for every character, is a real speed-up.

Lexical errors: Few errors can be caught by the lexer alone, because it sees only small pieces of text. If it reads fi ( a == f(x)), it cannot know whether fi is a misspelled if or a function name; it simply returns an id and leaves the decision to the parser. True lexical errors are things like a character that cannot start any token (such as @ or a stray backtick in C), a string literal or comment that never closes before the end of the file, or a number that is malformed such as 12.3.4.

Recovering from lexical errors: The simplest strategy is panic mode: delete characters from the input until the lexer can find a well-formed token again, then continue. Other small repairs are possible: delete one extra character, insert a missing character, replace one character with another, or swap two neighbouring characters. A compiler might try the single change that turns the input into a valid lexeme. Most real compilers just report the error with a line and column number and skip the bad character.

Real life example 1, a mobile number validator: A form on a Bangladeshi e-commerce site asks for a phone number. Behind the scenes, a small scanner reads the characters you typed, removes spaces and dashes, and checks the pattern: optional +88, then 01, then a digit from 3 to 9, then eight more digits. If you type 01712-345678, the scanner removes the dash and accepts 01712345678 as one token of type phone number. This is a tiny lexer in action: characters in, one classified token out.

Real life example 2, an SMS banking command: Some banking services let customers send SMS commands like BAL 1234 or TRF 01711000000 500. The server's first job is to split the message into tokens: a keyword (BAL or TRF), a PIN or phone number, and an amount. Spaces are skipped, letters are case-folded, and an unknown keyword triggers an error reply. After lexing, a tiny parser checks that TRF is followed by exactly a phone number and an amount.

Common mistakes: Students mix up token and lexeme; remember, the token is the category and the lexeme is the actual text. Many forget that the lexer returns attributes, not just names. Another mistake is to think the lexer checks that brackets are balanced; it does not, that needs a grammar and is the parser's job. Some think the lexer must produce the whole token list before parsing starts; usually it is called on demand.

What exams ask: Explain the role of the lexical analyzer and its interaction with the parser. Define token, lexeme and pattern with examples. Count the tokens in a given C statement, such as printf statements or if statements. Explain input buffering with buffer pairs and sentinels and why sentinels help. List lexical errors and recovery methods. Give reasons for separating lexical analysis from parsing.

Recap: The lexer is the compiler's word-cutter. It reads characters, skips spaces and comments, and returns tokens with attributes when the parser asks. Token is the category, lexeme the text, pattern the rule. Buffer pairs with sentinels make reading fast with only one test per character. Lexical errors are few, and panic mode is the simplest recovery. Next lesson we write the patterns precisely using regular definitions and draw transition diagrams that recognise them.
key_points: The lexer reads characters and returns tokens to the parser on demand, skipping white space and comments.
Token = category (name plus attribute), lexeme = actual text, pattern = rule describing the lexemes.
Identifiers carry a symbol-table pointer as their attribute; relops carry which operator they are.
Lexing is separated from parsing for simplicity, efficiency and portability.
Lookahead and retracting are needed to tell > from >=.
Buffer pairs read N characters at a time; sentinels reduce two tests per character to one.
Lexical errors include illegal characters and unterminated strings; panic mode deletes characters until a valid token appears.
lessons.tip: When counting tokens in an exam, go left to right and write each token in angle brackets. Do not forget brackets, commas and the final semicolon; they are all tokens.
lessons.task: Take the line while (i < n) { sum = sum + a[i]; i++; } and write its full token stream with attributes. Count the tokens, then compare with a friend's count and find any difference.

quiz.q: In the statement total = total + 1, what is total?
options: A lexeme of the token id
quiz.explain: total is the actual text in the source; it matches the pattern for identifiers, so it is a lexeme of token id.

quiz.q: How many tokens are in: if (x >= 10) y = 1;
quiz.explain: if, (, x, >=, 10, ), y, =, 1, ; makes 10 tokens.

quiz.q: Why are sentinels used in input buffering?
options: To reduce the two checks per character to one
quiz.explain: With an eof sentinel at each buffer end, the loop only checks for eof, then decides why it appeared.

quiz.q: Which of these is usually NOT the lexer's job?
options: Entering identifiers into the symbol table
quiz.explain: Balanced brackets need a context-free grammar; that is the parser's job.

quiz.q: When the lexer reads > and then a letter, what must it do?
options: Return > and retract the extra character
quiz.explain: It read one character too many; it returns > and pushes the letter back for the next token.

lessons.title: Specifying and Recognizing Tokens
lessons.content:
Think of the security guard at the gate of a Dhaka apartment building. He has a written rule book: residents have a card with a flat number, guests must give a name and the flat they are visiting, delivery riders must show an app order. For each person who walks up, the guard follows a small mental flowchart: card? yes, let in; no card, ask for name; name and flat given, call the flat. A lexer works the same way. First we write the rules for each kind of token precisely, then we turn each rule into a flowchart the machine can follow character by character.

Two steps: This lesson has two halves. Specifying tokens means writing exact, unambiguous descriptions of what each token looks like. For this we use regular expressions, which you already know from Theory of Computation. Recognizing tokens means building something that reads characters and decides which token they form. For this we use transition diagrams, a drawing very close to a finite automaton. In the next lesson we will see how a tool turns the specification straight into a recognizer automatically.

Regular expressions, a quick recap: A regular expression describes a set of strings. The basic pieces are a single symbol such as a, the empty string ε, union written r|s (r or s), concatenation rs (r followed by s) and Kleene star r* (zero or more copies of r). Star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union, so ab*|c means (a(b*))|c. For example, (0|1)*1 means any binary string ending in 1. We will not re-prove anything here; we will just use these as a precise language for patterns.

Useful shorthands: Real tools add a few conveniences that do not add power but save typing. r+ means one or more copies of r, so r+ is the same as rr*. r? means zero or one copy, the same as r|ε. A character class like [a-z] means any one lowercase letter, and [0-9] any digit. [A-Za-z_] is any letter or underscore. These shorthands appear in every lexer generator and in regular expressions used by programming languages.

Regular definitions: Writing one giant regular expression for every token is unreadable. Instead we give names to smaller expressions and build bigger ones from them, like defining helper functions. This list of named expressions is called a regular definition. The only rule is that each name may use only names defined before it, so there is no recursion. Recursion would take us beyond regular languages into context-free ones.

Identifiers as a regular definition: In C, an identifier starts with a letter or underscore and continues with letters, digits or underscores. We write: letter_ -> [A-Za-z_]; digit -> [0-9]; id -> letter_ ( letter_ | digit )*. Check it on examples: total matches; _count matches; x9 matches; 9x does not, because it starts with a digit. Exactly what C wants.

Numbers as a regular definition: Unsigned numbers like 5280, 0.01234, 6.336E4 or 1.89E-4 need more care. We write: digits -> digit+; optionalFraction -> ( . digits )?; optionalExponent -> ( E ( + | - )? digits )?; number -> digits optionalFraction optionalExponent. Check 1.89E-4: digits matches 1, optionalFraction matches .89, optionalExponent matches E-4. Check 6.: digits matches 6, but a dot must be followed by digits, so 6. alone is not a number under this definition. Check .5: it does not start with digits, so this definition rejects it, even though some languages accept it. A definition is a design decision.

White space and other tokens: We also need ws -> ( blank | tab | newline )+. When the lexer matches ws, it does not return anything to the parser; it simply starts looking for the next token. Relational operators are a short list: relop -> < | > | <= | >= | = | <>, in the Pascal style used by the textbook, where = means equal and <> means not equal. Keywords such as if, then and else are just their own spelling.

Transition diagrams: A transition diagram is a flowchart made of circles called states and arrows called edges. Each edge is labelled with a character or a set of characters. One state is the start state. Some states are accepting states, drawn with double circles, meaning a lexeme has been found. Some accepting states have a star next to them, which means the lexer read one character too many and must retract the forward pointer by one before returning the token.

Diagram for relop: Start in state 0. On < go to state 1. From state 1: on = go to state 2 and return (relop, LE); on > go to state 3 and return (relop, NE); on any other character go to state 4, marked with a star, retract and return (relop, LT). From state 0 on = go to state 5 and return (relop, EQ). From state 0 on > go to state 6. From state 6: on = go to state 7 and return (relop, GE); on any other character go to state 8 with a star, retract and return (relop, GT). Nine states recognise six operators, with lookahead where needed.

Tracing the relop diagram: Input is a<=b. Suppose the lexer has already returned a and is now at <. State 0 reads < and moves to state 1. State 1 reads = and moves to state 2, which accepts and returns (relop, LE) with no retraction. The next token starts at b. Now input a<b. At state 1 the next character is b, which is other, so we go to state 4, retract one character so that b is not lost, and return (relop, LT).

Diagram for identifiers: From the start state, a letter leads to state 10. State 10 loops back to itself on any letter or digit. On any other character it moves to an accepting state with a star: retract, then return the token. To return it, the lexer calls something like installID, which looks up the lexeme in the symbol table, adds it if new, and returns a pointer, and getToken, which says whether this lexeme is a keyword or an ordinary id.

Keywords vs identifiers: The keyword if also matches the id pattern. How do we keep them apart? The common, simple method is to put all reserved words into the symbol table before lexing begins, each marked with its token name. When the id diagram finds the lexeme if, the lookup finds the entry marked as keyword if and returns that token. An ordinary name like ifx is not in the table as a keyword, so it becomes an id. The other method is to draw a separate diagram for each keyword and give keywords priority, but that becomes messy with many keywords.

Diagram for numbers: The number diagram follows the regular definition. From the start, digits loop in one state; this state can accept an integer. A dot leads to a state that must see at least one digit; then digits loop again and can accept a fraction. An E leads to a state that may see + or -, then must see at least one digit, then digits loop and accept. Every accepting exit in this diagram is starred because the lexer only knows a number has ended after reading a character that cannot continue it.

Tracing a number: Input 12.5E-3 followed by a space. Read 1, 2: in the digits loop. Read the dot: move to the fraction state. Read 5: fraction digits. Read E: exponent state. Read -: sign seen. Read 3: exponent digits. Read space: other, so accept with retraction and return (number, 0.0125). The attribute here is the numeric value. If instead the input were 12E followed by a space, after E the diagram needs a sign or a digit and gets a space. Since no accepting state is reached, the lexer falls back to the last accepting point, which was after 12, and returns 12, giving back E and the space.

Longest match rule: When the lexer could stop at more than one place, it chooses the longest possible lexeme. That is why <= is one token and not < followed by =, and why ifx is an identifier and not the keyword if followed by x. Longest match is also why 12.5 is one number and not 12 followed by .5. To implement it, the lexer keeps reading as long as some pattern can still match and remembers the last position where a full match happened.

Priority rule: When two patterns match the same longest lexeme, the one listed first wins. In a lexer specification we list keyword rules before the identifier rule, so if matches the keyword. This rule plus longest match together remove all ambiguity: for any input, there is exactly one way to cut it into tokens.

Combining diagrams: A real lexer has diagrams for many tokens. There are three ways to run them. One: try them one after another; if a diagram fails, reset forward to lexemeBegin and try the next. Two: run them in parallel, feeding each character to all diagrams, and pick the longest match. Three, the best: combine all diagrams into one big diagram, then into one DFA, so that each character is read once. Lesson 5 shows how this is done automatically.

Real life example 1, Bangladesh NID numbers: A government form must check national ID numbers. A regular definition says: nid -> digit{10} | digit{13} | digit{17}, using a common shorthand for exact repetition, because older and newer cards have different lengths. A transition diagram counts digits and accepts only at counts 10, 13 or 17. The form rejects 12 digits immediately, before any database lookup, saving time and cost.

Real life example 2, price tags in a supermarket app: An app reads price tags from scanned text such as Tk 1,250.50. A regular definition like price -> Tk ws? [0-9]{1,3} ( , [0-9]{3} )* ( . [0-9]{2} )? describes it, with a matching diagram. Longest match ensures 1,250.50 is read as one price and not 1 followed by other bits. This is precisely the kind of pattern work lexers do all day.

Common mistakes: Students often forget the star on accepting states and so lose the extra character. Some write recursive regular definitions, which are not allowed. Many forget that keywords also match the id pattern, so they need a reserved word table or priority. Others draw diagrams that accept 1. or .E5 when the definition does not allow them. Always test a diagram with two good and two bad strings.

What exams ask: Write regular definitions for identifiers, unsigned numbers and relational operators. Draw transition diagrams for relop, identifiers and unsigned numbers and explain the star states. Explain how keywords are separated from identifiers. Explain longest match and rule priority with examples. Trace a given input through a diagram.

Recap: Regular expressions and regular definitions specify tokens precisely; shorthands like +, ? and [a-z] save effort. Transition diagrams recognise tokens character by character, with starred states that retract one character. Keywords are separated from identifiers by a reserved word table. Longest match and first-rule priority make tokenisation unique. Next lesson we let the machine build an efficient DFA from the regular expressions and look at the Lex tool.
key_points: Specify tokens with regular expressions and named regular definitions; recognise them with transition diagrams.
Shorthands: r+ = rr*, r? = r|ε, [a-z] is a character class; they add convenience, not power.
id -> letter_ ( letter_ | digit )* and number -> digits ( . digits )? ( E ( + | - )? digits )?.
A starred accepting state means the lexer read one extra character and must retract it.
The relop diagram uses lookahead to tell < from <= and <>, and > from >=.
Keywords are kept apart from identifiers by preloading reserved words in the symbol table or giving them priority.
Longest match picks the longest lexeme; on a tie, the rule listed first wins.
lessons.tip: For every regular definition you write, test it on two strings that must match and two that must not. Most exam mistakes are caught by this one-minute check.
lessons.task: Write a regular definition for Bangladeshi mobile numbers (optional +88, then 01, then a digit 3-9, then 8 digits). Draw its transition diagram on paper and trace +8801712345678, 01512345678 and 0171234567.

quiz.q: What does a star next to an accepting state mean in a transition diagram?
options: The lexer must retract one character before returning the token
quiz.explain: The lexer read one character beyond the lexeme, so it moves the forward pointer back by one.

quiz.q: Which string matches number -> digits ( . digits )? ( E ( + | - )? digits )?
quiz.explain: 1, then .89, then E-4 fit the three parts; the others break the definition.

quiz.q: Why is ifx returned as an identifier, not as keyword if followed by x?
options: Because if is not a keyword
Because of the longest match rule
quiz.explain: The lexer chooses the longest lexeme; ifx as one id is longer than if.

quiz.q: A common way to separate keywords from identifiers is to:
options: Write keywords in capital letters only
Preload reserved words into the symbol table
quiz.explain: When the id diagram finds a lexeme, the lookup shows whether it is a reserved word.

quiz.q: Which is NOT allowed in a regular definition?
options: A name defined in terms of itself
quiz.explain: Recursion would leave regular languages; each name may only use earlier names.

lessons.title: From Regular Expressions to a Lexer, and Lex
lessons.content:
Imagine you run a busy courier office in Chattogram that sorts parcels by address. At first you hire a person who reads each address and thinks hard about every rule. It works, but slowly. Then someone builds a sorting machine: all the rules are converted once into a fixed set of chutes, and each parcel just slides down the right path without anyone thinking. A lexer generator does the same for tokens. You write the rules once as regular expressions, and a tool converts them into a deterministic automaton that classifies characters at full speed.

The goal: In lesson 4 we drew transition diagrams by hand. For a real language with dozens of tokens that is slow and error-prone. We want an automatic pipeline: regular expressions in, a fast deterministic finite automaton (DFA) out, plus a small driver loop that runs the DFA over the input. Theory of Computation already proved that every regular expression has an equivalent DFA. Here we care about the practical construction and how a lexer uses it.

Route 1, recap of Thompson and subsets: The classic route has two steps. First, Thompson's construction turns a regular expression into an NFA with ε-moves. It builds small NFAs for single symbols and glues them together for union, concatenation and star, so the NFA has at most about two states for each symbol and operator. Second, the subset construction turns the NFA into a DFA, where each DFA state is a set of NFA states, using ε-closure and move. You practised both in Theory of Computation, so we will not repeat the steps. For (a|b)*abb this route gives a DFA with 5 states, which minimisation reduces to 4.

Route 2, directly from a regular expression: Compilers often use a neater method that skips the NFA entirely and goes straight from the regular expression to a DFA. It works on the syntax tree of the expression and computes four functions called nullable, firstpos, lastpos and followpos. Let us learn it on the same example, (a|b)*abb, because it is a favourite exam question.

Step 1, augment and number: Add a special end marker # to the end, giving (a|b)*abb#. The # marks where a match is complete. Now number every leaf that holds a symbol, left to right: a is position 1, b is position 2, then a is 3, b is 4, b is 5 and # is 6. Build the syntax tree: a star node over an or node of 1 and 2, then concatenation nodes joining in 3, 4, 5 and 6.

Step 2, nullable: nullable(n) is true if the subtree at n can generate the empty string. A leaf with a symbol is not nullable. A star node is always nullable, since zero copies is allowed. An or node is nullable if either child is. A concatenation node is nullable only if both children are. In our tree, only the star node and its parent chain until the first symbol are relevant: the star node is nullable, but every concatenation that includes a, b or # is not.

Step 3, firstpos and lastpos: firstpos(n) is the set of positions that can be the first symbol of a string generated by n; lastpos(n) is the set that can be last. For a leaf at position i, both are {i}. For an or node, take the union of the children. For a star node, they equal the child's sets. For a concatenation c1 c2: firstpos is firstpos(c1), plus firstpos(c2) if c1 is nullable; lastpos is lastpos(c2), plus lastpos(c1) if c2 is nullable. For our tree, the star node has firstpos {1,2}, and because it is nullable, the concatenation with position 3 has firstpos {1,2,3}. That is the firstpos of the whole tree.

Step 4, followpos: followpos(i) is the set of positions that can come right after position i in some string. Only two rules create it. Rule one, for a concatenation c1 c2: every position in lastpos(c1) is followed by everything in firstpos(c2). Rule two, for a star node n: every position in lastpos(n) is followed by everything in firstpos(n), because the star can loop. Applying them: followpos(1) = {1,2,3}, followpos(2) = {1,2,3}, followpos(3) = {4}, followpos(4) = {5}, followpos(5) = {6}, and followpos(6) is empty.

Step 5, build the DFA: The start state is firstpos of the root, A = {1,2,3}. For each state S and each symbol x, look at positions in S that hold x and take the union of their followpos sets. From A on a: positions 1 and 3 hold a, so we get followpos(1) union followpos(3) = {1,2,3,4}; call it B. From A on b: position 2 holds b, giving {1,2,3}, which is A again. From B on a: again 1 and 3, giving B. From B on b: positions 2 and 4, giving {1,2,3,5}; call it C. From C on a: B. From C on b: positions 2 and 5, giving {1,2,3,6}; call it D. From D on a: B. From D on b: position 2 only, giving A.

The result: We have four states A, B, C, D. Any state containing position 6, the # marker, is accepting, so D is the only accepting state. Check it on abb: A to B on a, B to C on b, C to D on b, accept. Check on aabb: A, B, B, C, D, accept. Check on abab: A, B, C, B, C, not accepting, correct because it does not end in abb. This direct method gave the minimal 4-state DFA immediately, without building an NFA.

Minimising the DFA: The routes above may produce extra equivalent states. Minimisation, which you learned with the table-filling method, merges states that behave identically for every future input. For a lexer, there is one twist: accepting states that return different tokens must start in different groups, because they are not interchangeable even if their futures look alike. A state that returns id must never be merged with one that returns number.

Many tokens, one DFA: A lexer must recognise many patterns at once: keywords, identifiers, numbers, operators. The generator combines all regular expressions into one big NFA with a new start state that has ε-edges to each pattern's NFA, then converts it to one DFA. Each accepting DFA state remembers which patterns it accepts. If it accepts several, the pattern listed first in the specification wins, which is the priority rule from lesson 4.

The driver loop: The DFA is stored as a table move[state][character]. The lexer runs a simple loop: start at the start state; read a character; look up the next state; if it is accepting, remember this state and the input position as the last match; continue until the table says there is no move, called the dead state. Then go back to the last remembered match, return its token, and set the input pointer just after that lexeme. This implements longest match exactly. With 128 or 256 possible characters, the table can be large, so real generators compress it, for example by grouping characters that always behave the same into classes.

Lex and Flex: Lex was written at Bell Labs in the 1970s; Flex (fast lex) is the free version widely used today. You write a specification file, usually ending in .l. The tool produces a C file, lex.yy.c, containing the DFA tables and a function yylex(). You compile that C file with a C compiler and get a working lexer. The parser, usually made by Yacc or Bison, calls yylex() each time it needs a token.

The Lex file structure: A Lex file has three parts separated by lines containing %%. The first part is declarations: C code to copy into the output between %{ and %}, plus regular definitions such as digit [0-9] and letter [A-Za-z]. The second part is the translation rules, each a pattern followed by an action in braces, for example {digit}+ { yylval = atoi(yytext); return NUMBER; } or a rule matching if that returns the token IF. The third part is auxiliary C functions, such as installID, used by the actions.

Useful Lex names: yytext points to the characters of the current lexeme, and yyleng is its length. yylval is a variable for passing the attribute value to the parser. If an action does not return, for example the rule for white space whose action is empty, the lexer simply continues to the next lexeme. Lex resolves conflicts exactly as we described: it prefers the longest match, and on a tie it picks the rule listed first, so keyword rules go above the identifier rule.

A tiny Lex walk-through: Suppose the rules are, in order: white space with an empty action; if returning IF; identifiers returning ID; digits returning NUMBER; and the character + returning PLUS. On input if x1+42, the lexer skips nothing at first, matches if for both the IF rule and the ID rule with equal length, chooses IF because it is first, then skips the space, matches x1 as ID, + as PLUS and 42 as NUMBER with yylval set to 42. The parser receives IF, ID, PLUS, NUMBER.

Real life example 1, log file analysis: A system admin at a mobile operator in Dhaka must scan huge log files for patterns such as IP addresses, error codes and phone numbers. Tools like grep compile regular expressions into automata in a similar way and then stream gigabytes of text through them. The same idea that makes a compiler's lexer fast makes this search fast.

Real life example 2, a Bangla transliteration keyboard: Phonetic keyboards let you type ami bhalo achi in English letters and get Bangla script. Under the hood, the input is split into chunks such as bh, a, l, o using longest match, so that bh becomes one Bangla letter instead of b plus h. That is a lexer with longest match and priority, built from a table of patterns.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the # end marker in the direct method, so you cannot tell which states accept. Computing firstpos of a concatenation without checking if the left child is nullable. Applying the star rule for followpos to positions that are not in lastpos of the star node. In Lex, putting the identifier rule above keyword rules, which makes every keyword an identifier. Also, forgetting that an action without return makes the lexer continue silently.

What exams ask: Construct a DFA directly from a regular expression such as (a|b)*abb using nullable, firstpos, lastpos and followpos, showing the syntax tree and followpos table. Convert a regular expression to an NFA with Thompson's construction and then to a DFA. Explain the structure of a Lex program with an example. Explain how Lex resolves conflicts.

Recap: A lexer generator turns regular expressions into one DFA, either through Thompson and subset construction or directly via followpos. For (a|b)*abb the direct method gives the 4-state DFA A, B, C, D with D accepting. A driver loop runs the DFA, remembers the last accepting position and returns the longest match. Lex and Flex package all of this: you write patterns and actions, and they write the C lexer. Next lesson we move to phase two, the parser.
key_points: A lexer generator converts regular expressions into one DFA plus a driver loop.
Route 1: Thompson's construction to an NFA, then subset construction to a DFA, then minimisation.
Route 2 (direct): augment with #, number positions, compute nullable, firstpos, lastpos and followpos.
followpos comes only from concatenation (lastpos(c1) to firstpos(c2)) and star (lastpos(n) to firstpos(n)).
For (a|b)*abb the direct method gives 4 states; the state containing the # position accepts.
The driver remembers the last accepting position to implement longest match.
A Lex file has declarations, %% rules with actions, %% auxiliary code; yytext, yyleng, yylval and yylex() are its key names.
lessons.tip: In the direct method, write the followpos table first and double-check it. Once the table is right, building the DFA is mechanical and quick.
lessons.task: Using the direct method, build the DFA for (a|b)*ab# on paper: number the positions, compute followpos, and build the states. Then trace the strings ab, bab and abb through your DFA.

quiz.q: Why is the marker # added to the end of the regular expression in the direct method?
options: To mark where a complete match ends, so accepting states can be identified
quiz.explain: Any DFA state containing the position of # is an accepting state.

quiz.q: For (a|b)*abb# with positions a1 b2 a3 b4 b5 #6, what is followpos(3)?
quiz.explain: Position 3 (a) is followed by position 4 (b) in the concatenation.

quiz.q: In the direct method, what is the start state of the DFA?
quiz.explain: The start state is the set of positions that can begin a string, firstpos(root), here {1,2,3}.

quiz.q: If an input matches both the keyword rule and the identifier rule with the same length, Lex chooses:
options: The rule listed first in the file
quiz.explain: On a tie in length, Lex uses the earlier rule, so keyword rules are placed above the identifier rule.

quiz.q: In a Lex action, what does yytext hold?
options: The characters of the current lexeme
The name of the input file
quiz.explain: yytext points to the matched lexeme; yyleng gives its length.

lessons.title: Syntax Analysis: Grammars, Parse Trees and Errors
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket umpire. He does not care whether each ball is beautiful; he checks whether the whole sequence of events follows the rules. Six legal balls make an over. A wide does not count. The bowler must change ends after each over. He watches the stream of events and either says fine, carry on, or raises a hand and calls a problem. The parser is the umpire of the compiler. The lexer hands it a stream of tokens, and the parser checks whether that stream follows the grammar of the language, building a picture of the structure as it goes.

What the parser does: The syntax analyzer, or parser, takes tokens from the lexer and checks that they can be generated by the grammar of the source language. If they can, it produces a parse tree, or more often an abstract syntax tree, that shows how the program is structured: which expressions belong to which statement, which statements are inside which loop. If they cannot, it reports syntax errors in a useful way and tries to continue. In many compilers the parser is also the boss that drives the other front-end phases, calling the lexer for tokens and triggering semantic actions.

Why not just regular expressions: Regular expressions were perfect for tokens, but they cannot describe nesting. A language like C allows brackets inside brackets inside brackets, if statements inside loops inside functions, to any depth. To check that every ( has a matching ), a machine needs unlimited memory of how many are open, and a finite automaton has only finitely many states. You saw this in Theory of Computation: balanced brackets are not regular. That is why the syntax of programming languages is described with context-free grammars, which are recognised by stack-based machines.

Context-free grammars, a quick recap: A grammar has terminals (the tokens, such as id, +, if), nonterminals (syntactic variables such as Expr or Stmt), a start symbol, and productions of the form A -> α, where A is a nonterminal and α is a string of terminals and nonterminals. Programming language manuals write grammars in BNF or EBNF, for example stmt -> if ( expr ) stmt else stmt. We use the convention that capital letters like E, T, F are nonterminals and lowercase or symbols like id and + are terminals.

Derivations: A derivation starts from the start symbol and repeatedly replaces a nonterminal with the right side of one of its productions until only terminals remain. In a leftmost derivation we always replace the leftmost nonterminal; in a rightmost derivation the rightmost one. These two orders matter because top-down parsers trace leftmost derivations, and bottom-up parsers trace rightmost derivations backwards. Each intermediate string is called a sentential form.

Our main grammar: Throughout this course we use the expression grammar G1: E -> E + T | T; T -> T * F | F; F -> ( E ) | id. Here E is an expression, T is a term and F is a factor. Leftmost derivation of id + id * id: E => E + T => T + T => F + T => id + T => id + T * F => id + F * F => id + id * F => id + id * id. Eight steps, each replacing the leftmost nonterminal.

Parse trees: A parse tree shows a derivation as a picture, forgetting the order of replacements. The root is the start symbol, each interior node is a nonterminal whose children are the right side of the production used, and the leaves, read left to right, give the input string, called the yield. For id + id * id under G1, the root E has children E, +, T. The left E becomes T, then F, then id. The right T has children T, *, F, which become id and id. So the * subtree hangs below the + node, which means multiplication is done first. The tree is the parser's real output.

Ambiguity: A grammar is ambiguous if some string has more than one parse tree, or equivalently more than one leftmost derivation. Consider G2: E -> E + E | E * E | ( E ) | id. For id + id * id, one tree puts + at the root with id * id as its right child, meaning id + (id * id). Another tree puts * at the root with id + id as its left child, meaning (id + id) * id. With numbers 2 + 3 * 4, the first gives 14 and the second gives 20. A compiler cannot accept a grammar where the same code can mean two different things.

Removing ambiguity with precedence levels: G1 is the unambiguous version of G2. The trick is to create one nonterminal per precedence level. Operators with lower precedence, like +, appear in rules closer to the start symbol; operators with higher precedence, like *, appear in rules further down. Because a T can never directly contain a bare + without brackets, any + must sit above all * in the tree. Brackets reset the levels through F -> ( E ). If we added exponentiation with even higher precedence, we would add another level below F.

Associativity: For id - id - id, should it mean (id - id) - id or id - (id - id)? With numbers 10 - 4 - 3, the first gives 3 and the second gives 9. Arithmetic requires left associativity, which a grammar gets from left recursion: E -> E - T puts the earlier minus deeper on the left, so it is done first. Exponentiation is usually right associative: 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 means 2 ^ (3 ^ 2) = 512, which we get from right recursion, P -> B ^ P | B. So the shape of the recursion encodes associativity.

The dangling else: The grammar stmt -> if expr then stmt | if expr then stmt else stmt | other is ambiguous. In if E1 then if E2 then S1 else S2, the else could belong to the inner if or the outer if. Almost all languages choose the rule: match each else with the closest unmatched then. It is possible to rewrite the grammar with matched and unmatched statements to force this, but the rewritten grammar is clumsy. In practice, parser generators keep the ambiguous grammar and resolve the conflict by preferring to shift the else, which attaches it to the nearest if; we will see this in lesson 14.

Kinds of parsers: Universal parsing methods such as CYK and Earley can parse any context-free grammar but take up to cubic time in the length of the input, too slow for compilers. Real compilers use two families that run in linear time on suitable grammars. Top-down parsers build the tree from the root down to the leaves, guessing productions from the next token; LL parsers and recursive descent belong here. Bottom-up parsers build from the leaves up to the root, combining pieces when they are complete; LR parsers, including SLR and LALR, belong here. Both read the input left to right, one token at a time.

Types of programming errors: Lexical errors are misspelled tokens or illegal characters. Syntactic errors are things like a missing semicolon, an extra brace, or a case outside any switch. Semantic errors are type mismatches or using an undeclared name. Logical errors are wrong programs that are perfectly legal, such as writing = instead of == in a C condition, which no compiler phase can always detect. The parser is responsible for syntactic errors, and modern LL and LR parsers have the viable-prefix property: they detect an error as soon as the input read so far cannot be the beginning of any valid program.

Goals of error handling: Report errors clearly and accurately, ideally with line and column numbers. Recover quickly enough to find more errors in the same run. Add little cost to compiling correct programs, which are the common case. These goals pull against each other: trying too hard to recover can produce a flood of confusing secondary errors.

Panic-mode recovery: On finding an error, the parser throws away input tokens one at a time until it finds a synchronising token, usually a delimiter such as a semicolon or a closing brace, whose role is clear. It then adjusts its stack and continues. Panic mode is simple and can never loop forever, but it may skip a lot of input and miss errors in the skipped part. It is the most widely used strategy.

Phrase-level recovery: The parser makes a small local correction to the remaining input so it can continue, such as replacing a comma with a semicolon, deleting an extra semicolon or inserting a missing one. These corrections are chosen by the compiler writer for common situations. The danger is that an insertion could make the parser loop, inserting forever, so it must be designed carefully.

Error productions and global correction: With error productions, the compiler writer adds grammar rules for common mistakes, for example a rule that accepts a missing semicolon before a closing brace, so the parser can recognise the mistake and give a precise message. Global correction tries to find the smallest set of insertions, deletions and changes that turns the program into a valid one. It is interesting in theory but too costly in practice, and the closest valid program is not always what the programmer meant.

Real life example 1, a bKash-style USSD menu: When you dial a USSD code, the server expects a sequence of steps: menu choice, then number, then amount, then reference, then PIN. That sequence is a tiny grammar. If you enter an amount where a phone number is expected, the server detects the error immediately and asks again, instead of continuing with nonsense. That is a parser with the viable-prefix property and phrase-level recovery.

Real life example 2, a spreadsheet formula: In a spreadsheet you type =SUM(A1:A10)*(1+B2. The formula bar shows an error because a bracket is unclosed. The spreadsheet parser uses an expression grammar much like G1, with function calls and ranges added, to know that * binds tighter than + and that brackets must match. It even offers to insert the missing bracket, a phrase-level fix.

Common mistakes: Students think removing ambiguity changes the language; it should not, it only gives each string exactly one tree. Many forget that left recursion gives left associativity and right recursion gives right associativity. Some show an ambiguous grammar by giving two derivations that are just different orders of the same tree; you must show two different trees or two different leftmost derivations. Others confuse syntax errors with semantic ones.

What exams ask: Define ambiguity and show that E -> E + E | E * E | id is ambiguous using id + id * id. Write an unambiguous grammar for arithmetic expressions with correct precedence and associativity. Give leftmost and rightmost derivations and draw the parse tree. Explain the dangling else problem. Describe error recovery strategies: panic mode, phrase level, error productions and global correction.

Recap: The parser checks the token stream against a context-free grammar and builds a tree. Derivations and parse trees show structure; an ambiguous grammar gives two trees for one string. Precedence comes from grammar levels, associativity from the direction of recursion. Compilers use linear-time top-down or bottom-up parsers and recover from errors mainly by panic mode and phrase-level fixes. Next lesson we start top-down parsing and learn how to prepare a grammar for it.
key_points: The parser checks tokens against a context-free grammar and builds a parse tree or syntax tree.
Regular expressions cannot describe nesting, so syntax needs context-free grammars and stack-based parsers.
A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two parse trees or two leftmost derivations.
E -> E + T | T, T -> T * F | F, F -> ( E ) | id is the unambiguous expression grammar: one nonterminal per precedence level.
Left recursion gives left associativity; right recursion gives right associativity.
The dangling else is resolved by matching each else with the nearest unmatched if.
Error recovery: panic mode (skip to a synchronising token), phrase level, error productions, global correction.
lessons.tip: To prove a grammar is ambiguous, draw two full parse trees side by side for the same string. A picture of two different trees is the clearest proof an examiner can ask for.
lessons.task: Using E -> E + T | T, T -> T * F | F, F -> ( E ) | id, write the leftmost and rightmost derivations of ( id + id ) * id and draw its parse tree. Then show the same string has two trees under E -> E + E | E * E | ( E ) | id, or explain why it does not.

quiz.q: Why can regular expressions not describe the full syntax of C?
options: They cannot handle unlimited nesting such as balanced brackets
quiz.explain: Matching brackets to any depth needs unbounded memory; finite automata have finite states.

quiz.q: A grammar is ambiguous when:
options: It has more than one nonterminal
Some string has two or more parse trees
quiz.explain: Two different parse trees (or leftmost derivations) for one string is the definition.

quiz.q: In E -> E + T | T, T -> T * F | F, why is * done before +?
options: Because * appears at a lower level of the grammar, deeper in the tree
quiz.explain: Higher-precedence operators appear in rules further from the start symbol, so they sit lower in the tree.

quiz.q: Which grammar shape gives right associativity, as needed for 2 ^ 3 ^ 2?
quiz.explain: Right recursion puts the later operator deeper, so it is evaluated first: 2 ^ (3 ^ 2).

quiz.q: What does panic-mode recovery do?
options: Inserts tokens until the program is valid
Finds the minimum number of changes
Skips tokens until a synchronising token such as ; is found
quiz.explain: It discards input up to a delimiter whose role is clear, then continues parsing.

lessons.title: Top-Down Parsing and Preparing the Grammar
lessons.content:
Think of planning a wedding in Bangladesh from the top. You start with the big goal, the wedding. You break it into parts: gaye holud, the wedding day, the reception. Each part breaks into smaller jobs: book the community centre, order the biriyani, print the cards. You keep breaking things down until each job is something concrete you can tick off. Top-down parsing works the same way. It starts with the start symbol of the grammar, the big goal, and keeps expanding it into smaller pieces until the pieces match the actual tokens of the input.

What top-down parsing is: A top-down parser builds the parse tree starting from the root and creating nodes in preorder, that is, parent before children, left before right. At each step it has a leftmost nonterminal to expand and must choose which production to use. Doing this produces a leftmost derivation of the input. The key question at every step is: which production should I pick for this nonterminal? The answer must come from looking at the next input token, called the lookahead.

Recursive descent: The most natural way to write a top-down parser by hand is recursive descent. You write one function for each nonterminal. The body of the function for A looks at the lookahead, chooses one production A -> X1 X2 ... Xk, and then handles each Xi in order: if Xi is a nonterminal it calls the function for Xi; if Xi is a terminal it checks that the lookahead equals Xi and moves to the next token, otherwise it reports an error. The call stack of the program acts as the parser's stack. Many production compilers, including GCC's C and C++ front ends and Clang, use hand-written recursive descent.

Backtracking: In the simplest form, if the parser picks a production and it fails later, it goes back, resets the input pointer and tries the next production. Example grammar: S -> c A d; A -> a b | a. Input: c a d. S matches c, then calls A. A tries a b: a matches, but b does not match d. So A backtracks, resets the input to a and tries the second choice a, which matches. Back in S, d matches d. Success. Backtracking works but can take exponential time on bad grammars and makes it hard to give good error messages, and undoing side effects such as symbol table entries is messy. Real compilers avoid it.

Predictive parsing: The better idea is to design the grammar so that the next token always tells us which production to use, with no guessing. Such a parser is called predictive. To make this possible, the grammar usually has to be prepared in two ways: remove left recursion and left factor it. Then in lessons 8 and 9 we will compute exactly which token predicts which production, using FIRST and FOLLOW sets.

The left recursion problem: Our grammar has E -> E + T. A recursive descent function E() would start by calling E() for the first symbol of the right side, without consuming any input. That call would again call E(), and so on, forever, until the stack overflows. A grammar is left recursive if some nonterminal A can derive a string that starts with A itself. Top-down parsers cannot handle left recursion, so we must rewrite the grammar to an equivalent one that has none.

Removing immediate left recursion: The basic pattern is A -> A α | β, where β does not start with A. This grammar generates β followed by any number of α, that is β α α α. We can generate the same strings with right recursion: A -> β A' and A' -> α A' | ε. The new nonterminal A' produces the tail of α's. More generally, if A -> A α1 | A α2 | ... | β1 | β2 | ..., then A -> β1 A' | β2 A' | ... and A' -> α1 A' | α2 A' | ... | ε.

Applying it to the expression grammar: For E -> E + T | T, here α is + T and β is T. So E -> T E' and E' -> + T E' | ε. For T -> T * F | F, α is * F and β is F, so T -> F T' and T' -> * F T' | ε. F -> ( E ) | id has no left recursion. The result is G3: E -> T E'; E' -> + T E' | ε; T -> F T'; T' -> * F T' | ε; F -> ( E ) | id. This is the most famous grammar in compiler exams. It generates exactly the same strings as before.

Indirect left recursion: Sometimes left recursion hides across rules. In S -> A a | b; A -> A c | S d | ε, S is not immediately left recursive, but S => A a => S d a, so S derives a string starting with S. The algorithm orders the nonterminals, here S then A. For each nonterminal, it first substitutes the productions of earlier nonterminals that appear at the start, then removes immediate left recursion.
