Why use an ambiguous grammar: The unambiguous expression grammar needs one nonterminal per precedence level, so a language with ten levels needs ten nonterminals and long chains of reductions like E -> T -> F just to handle a lone number. An ambiguous grammar like expr : expr '+' expr | expr '-' expr | expr '*' expr | expr '/' expr | '(' expr ')' | NUMBER ; is shorter, easier to read, gives fewer states and a faster parser. The only problem is that it produces shift/reduce conflicts. Yacc lets us resolve them with declarations instead of rewriting the grammar.

Precedence declarations: In the declarations section we write lines such as %left '+' '-' followed by %left '*' '/'. Each line gives its tokens the same precedence, and later lines have higher precedence. %left means left associative, %right means right associative, as for an exponent operator, and %nonassoc means the operator cannot be chained, as with comparison operators in some languages, so a < b < c is an error. Each rule gets the precedence of the last terminal in its body, unless we override it with %prec.

How Yacc uses precedence: When Yacc finds a shift/reduce conflict between reducing by rule R and shifting token a, it compares their precedences. If a has higher precedence, it shifts. If R has higher precedence, it reduces. If they are equal, it looks at associativity: left means reduce, right means shift, nonassoc means make it an error. Consider 2 + 3 * 4 with the ambiguous grammar. With expr + expr on the stack and * as the lookahead, the rule expr '+' expr has the precedence of +, which is lower than *, so Yacc shifts, and the multiplication happens first, giving 14. For 10 - 4 - 3, with expr - expr on the stack and - next, the precedences are equal and - is left associative, so Yacc reduces, giving (10 - 4) - 3 = 3.

Unary minus with %prec: The minus sign is used both as binary subtraction and as unary negation, as in -5 * 2. Unary minus should bind tighter than *. We declare an imaginary token with the highest precedence, for example %right UMINUS on the last precedence line, and write the rule expr : '-' expr %prec UMINUS { $$ = -$2; }. The %prec tells Yacc to give this rule the precedence of UMINUS instead of the precedence of '-'. So -5 * 2 is parsed as (-5) * 2.

The dangling else in Yacc: For stmt : IF '(' expr ')' stmt | IF '(' expr ')' stmt ELSE stmt, Yacc reports one shift/reduce conflict on ELSE. Its default rule for an unresolved shift/reduce conflict is to shift, which matches else with the nearest if, exactly what C wants. To silence the warning cleanly, a common trick is to declare %nonassoc LOWER_THAN_ELSE and then %nonassoc ELSE, and write the first alternative with %prec LOWER_THAN_ELSE. Now the rule has lower precedence than ELSE, so the tool shifts by design rather than by default.

Default conflict rules and reports: When precedence does not settle a conflict, Yacc uses two defaults: a shift/reduce conflict is resolved in favour of shift, and a reduce/reduce conflict in favour of the rule that appears first in the file. It reports how many conflicts it resolved this way. Running Yacc with the -v option, or Bison with --verbose, writes a text file describing every state, its items and actions, and the conflicts. Reading this file lets you find the exact state and token causing a conflict, using the item knowledge from lessons 11 to 13.

Error recovery with the error token: Yacc reserves a special token called error. You can write rules such as stmt : error ';' . When the parser hits a syntax error, it pops states off its stack until it finds a state that can shift the error token, shifts it, and then discards input tokens until it finds one that can legally follow, here the semicolon. Then it continues. This is panic-mode recovery chosen by the grammar writer. Calling the macro yyerrok in the action tells the parser that recovery is complete so that new errors are reported again immediately; normally Yacc suppresses messages until three tokens have been read successfully.

Lex and Yacc together: Run yacc with the -d option, or bison -d, to produce a header file with the token codes, such as y.tab.h. The Lex file includes this header so that its actions can return NUMBER, ID and so on with the same numeric codes. Run lex or flex on the .l file to get lex.yy.c. Compile both C files together with a C compiler into one program. At run time main() calls yyparse(), which calls yylex() repeatedly. The lexer sets yylval for tokens with values, and the parser's actions build results or syntax trees.

Typed values with %union: Real compilers need different kinds of values: numbers for constants, pointers to symbol table entries for identifiers, pointers to tree nodes for expressions. The %union declaration lists these kinds, %token <num> NUMBER says that NUMBER carries a number, and %type <node> expr says expr values are tree nodes. Yacc then checks that $1, $2 and $$ are used with the right types. This is how most compiler front ends built with Bison carry syntax trees upward.

Real life example 1, a university compiler lab: In many Bangladeshi universities, the compiler lab ends with a project such as a mini C or a Bangla-keyword language, where keywords like jodi and noyto replace if and else. Students write a Flex file for tokens and a Bison file with precedence declarations and actions that print three-address code. The theory from earlier lessons suddenly becomes a few hundred lines that actually translate programs.

Real life example 2, real software: Many well-known programs have used Yacc or Bison parsers, including the parsers of several database systems and scripting languages, and the GNU C compiler used a Bison-generated parser for C until it switched to a hand-written one. The tools remain popular for configuration languages, query languages and domain-specific languages in companies, because the grammar file doubles as clear documentation of the syntax.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that later precedence lines mean higher precedence. Writing actions that use $3 when the rule has only two symbols. Forgetting to set yylval in the lexer, so all numbers appear as 0 or garbage. Ignoring conflict counts reported by Yacc. Expecting %prec to work without declaring the token in a precedence line. And forgetting that the default action is $$ = $1.

What exams ask: Describe the structure of a Yacc program with an example, such as a desk calculator. Explain how Yacc resolves shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts, including precedence and associativity rules. Explain how ambiguous grammars are used with precedence declarations, the use of %prec for unary minus, and error recovery with the error token. Explain how Lex and Yacc work together.

Recap: Yacc and Bison turn a grammar with actions into an LALR(1) parser, yyparse(), that calls yylex() for tokens. Actions use $$ and $1, $2 to compute values bottom-up. Ambiguous grammars plus %left, %right, %nonassoc and %prec give small, fast parsers with the right precedence. Unresolved conflicts default to shift and to the earlier rule, and the error token enables panic-mode recovery. With parsing done, next lesson we attach meaning to grammars systematically through syntax-directed definitions.
key_points: Yacc (Bell Labs) and Bison (GNU) generate an LALR(1) parser yyparse() in C from a .y grammar file.
A Yacc file has declarations, %% grammar rules with C actions, %% supporting C code.
In actions, $$ is the left side's value and $1, $2, ... are right-side values; the default action is $$ = $1.
%left, %right and %nonassoc set associativity; later lines have higher precedence; a rule takes its last terminal's precedence.
Shift if the token's precedence is higher, reduce if the rule's is higher; on a tie use associativity.
Defaults: shift/reduce conflicts favour shift (dangling else), reduce/reduce favour the earlier rule; %prec handles unary minus.
The error token gives panic-mode recovery; yacc -d makes the token header shared with Lex, and yylval carries token values.
lessons.tip: Whenever Yacc reports conflicts, run it in verbose mode and read the output file state by state. Matching each conflict to the item sets you learned is the fastest way to fix a grammar.
lessons.task: On paper, write a Yacc file for a calculator supporting +, -, *, / and unary minus with correct precedence. Then work out by hand how your declarations resolve the conflicts in -2 * 3 + 4 and 8 / 4 / 2 and what values are printed.

quiz.q: In the action expr : expr '+' term { $$ = $1 + $3; }, what does $3 refer to?
options: The value of expr on the left side
The third rule in the file
quiz.explain: $1, $2 and $3 refer to the right-side symbols in order: expr, '+', term.

quiz.q: Given %left '+' '-' followed by %left '*' '/', which operator has higher precedence?
quiz.explain: Later precedence lines have higher precedence.

quiz.q: With expr - expr on the stack and - as lookahead, %left makes Yacc:
quiz.explain: Equal precedence with left associativity means reduce, giving (a - b) - c.

quiz.q: How does Yacc resolve an unresolved shift/reduce conflict by default?
quiz.explain: Shift is the default, which correctly handles the dangling else.

quiz.q: What is %prec UMINUS used for?
options: To give a rule a different precedence than its last terminal
quiz.explain: It lets unary minus use the high precedence of UMINUS instead of that of binary '-'.

lessons.title: Syntax-Directed Definitions and Attributes
lessons.content:
Think of a family tree drawn for a wedding invitation in Barishal. Some information flows upward: each family's total number of guests is the sum of the guests from its sub-families, and the grandparents' card shows the grand total. Some information flows downward: the family surname given at the top is passed down to every child's name card. A parse tree can carry information the same way. Values can be computed from the children and passed up, or handed down from the parent and siblings. A syntax-directed definition is the set of rules that says exactly how.

The idea: Parsing tells us the structure of the program, but a compiler needs more: values of constant expressions, types of expressions, addresses of variables, pieces of intermediate code. Syntax-directed translation attaches this information to grammar symbols and computes it using rules attached to productions. Because the rules follow the grammar, the translation is driven by the syntax, hence the name. Everything from type checking to intermediate code generation in the coming lessons is written this way.

Attributes: An attribute is any quantity associated with a grammar symbol: a number, a type, a string of code, a pointer to a symbol table entry or a tree node. We write X.a for attribute a of symbol X. For example E.val could be the numeric value of an expression, E.type its type and E.code the three-address code for it. Terminals usually have attributes provided by the lexer, such as digit.lexval for the numeric value of a digit.

Syntax-directed definitions: A syntax-directed definition, or SDD, is a context-free grammar together with attributes and semantic rules. Each production has a set of rules that compute attributes of the symbols in that production. For example, with production E -> E1 + T we write the rule E.val = E1.val + T.val. The subscript 1 in E1 just distinguishes the two occurrences of E in the same production. An SDD says what to compute, not in which order; the order is worked out from the dependencies.

Synthesized attributes: An attribute of a nonterminal A at a parse-tree node N is synthesized if it is computed by a rule of the production at N, the production with A on the left side, using only attribute values at N's children and at N itself. Information flows upward. E.val in E -> E1 + T is synthesized, because it uses the values of the children E1 and T. Terminals can have synthesized attributes too, but those come from the lexer.

Inherited attributes: An attribute of a nonterminal B at node N is inherited if it is computed by a rule of the production at N's parent, using attribute values at the parent, at N itself and at N's siblings. Information flows downward or sideways. Inherited attributes are useful when the meaning of a construct depends on its context, like the declared type that applies to every variable in a list, or the left operand that a later part of an expression needs.

The desk calculator SDD: Using the grammar with an end marker n: L -> E n has rule print(E.val). E -> E1 + T has E.val = E1.val + T.val. E -> T has E.val = T.val. T -> T1 * F has T.val = T1.val * F.val. T -> F has T.val = F.val. F -> ( E ) has F.val = E.val. F -> digit has F.val = digit.lexval. Every attribute here is synthesized. The print in the first rule is a side effect, which is allowed in an SDD; an SDD with no side effects at all is sometimes called an attribute grammar.

An annotated parse tree: A parse tree showing the values of attributes at its nodes is called an annotated parse tree. For the input 3 * 5 + 4 n: the leftmost digit 3 gives F.val = 3, then T.val = 3. The digit 5 gives F.val = 5. The node T -> T1 * F gives T.val = 3 * 5 = 15, and E -> T gives E.val = 15. On the right, digit 4 gives F.val = 4 and T.val = 4. The node E -> E1 + T gives E.val = 15 + 4 = 19, and L prints 19. Drawing this tree with each value written beside its node is a standard exam task.

Inherited attributes in declarations: Consider the C-like declaration int a, b, c. Grammar: D -> T L; T -> int; T -> float; L -> L1 , id; L -> id. Rules: T -> int has T.type = integer. T -> float has T.type = float. D -> T L has L.inh = T.type, passing the type down into the list. L -> L1 , id has L1.inh = L.inh, passing it further down, plus addType(id.entry, L.inh) to record the type of this identifier in the symbol table. L -> id has addType(id.entry, L.inh). Here L.inh is inherited: it comes from the sibling T through the parent D.

Tracing int a, b, c: T.type becomes integer. At D, L.inh = integer. The top L has the form L1 , id where id is c, so addType(c, integer) and its L1 gets inh = integer. That L1 is L1' , id with id b, so addType(b, integer), and so on down to the last L -> id with id a, giving addType(a, integer). All three variables get type integer, even though the type keyword appears only once at the start. Information flowed from the left sibling down to every identifier.

Inherited attributes after removing left recursion: In lesson 7 we saw that rewriting T -> T * F | F as T -> F T', T' -> * F T' | ε changes the tree shape. Inherited attributes repair the meaning. Rules: T -> F T' has T'.inh = F.val and T.val = T'.syn. T' -> * F T1' has T1'.inh = T'.inh * F.val and T'.syn = T1'.syn. T' -> ε has T'.syn = T'.inh. For 3 * 5, F gives 3, which is passed down as T'.inh = 3; the next T' multiplies by 5 and passes 15 down; the final empty T' copies 15 into syn, which flows back up to T.val = 15. The running product travels down as inh and comes back up as syn, which also restores left associativity for operators like minus.

Dependency graphs: To evaluate an SDD on a parse tree, we must compute each attribute after the attributes it depends on. A dependency graph has one node for each attribute instance in the tree and an edge from X.a to Y.b whenever a rule computes Y.b using X.a. For synthesized E.val in E -> E1 + T, there are edges from E1.val and T.val to E.val. For inherited L.inh in D -> T L, there is an edge from T.type to L.inh.

Evaluation order: Any topological sort of the dependency graph is a valid evaluation order: an ordering where every attribute comes after all attributes it depends on. If the graph has a cycle, there is no valid order and the SDD cannot be evaluated on that tree. Testing whether an arbitrary SDD can ever produce a cycle is expensive, so compilers stick to two classes of SDDs that are guaranteed to be safe and that fit well with parsing.

S-attributed definitions: An SDD is S-attributed if every attribute is synthesized. The desk calculator SDD is S-attributed. Such SDDs can be evaluated by any bottom-up order, for example a postorder traversal of the parse tree. Even better, they fit LR parsing perfectly: when the parser reduces by a production, the attributes of the right-side symbols are already known, so the left side's attributes can be computed at that moment, just as Yacc actions do with $$ = $1 + $3.

L-attributed definitions: An SDD is L-attributed if each attribute is either synthesized or, if it is an inherited attribute of Xi in a production A -> X1 X2 ... Xn, it depends only on inherited attributes of A, attributes of X1 to Xi-1 to the left of Xi, and attributes of Xi itself as long as no cycle is formed. The L stands for left: information flows from left to right, never from right to left. The declaration SDD and the T' SDD above are L-attributed. Every S-attributed SDD is also L-attributed. L-attributed SDDs can be evaluated in a single depth-first, left-to-right pass, which matches top-down parsing and recursive descent exactly.

An example that is not L-attributed: Suppose production A -> B C had the rule B.i = C.c. Here an inherited attribute of B depends on C, which is to its right. A left-to-right pass would reach B before C has been processed, so the rule breaks the L-attributed condition. Such rules are legal in an SDD but force multiple passes or building the whole tree first.

Real life example 1, a restaurant bill in Dhanmondi: Each item on the bill has a price, and each section's subtotal is the sum of its items: synthesized upward. The VAT rate, decided at the top of the bill by the restaurant's category, is applied to every line: inherited downward. The final total is synthesized from the subtotals plus VAT. A billing system written as rules on a tree of sections and items is a syntax-directed definition in disguise.

Real life example 2, a university result sheet: A department's result system has a tree: department, batch, student, course. The grading scale, chosen by the university, is inherited down to every course. Each course's grade point is synthesized from marks, each student's CGPA is synthesized from courses and credits, and the batch's average is synthesized from students. Changing the grading scale at the top changes everything below it, through inherited attributes.

Common mistakes: Calling an attribute synthesized just because it belongs to the left side; you must check where its values come from. Writing rules where an inherited attribute depends on symbols to its right and then claiming the SDD is L-attributed. Forgetting the base rule T' -> ε with T'.syn = T'.inh, which leaves the result stuck at the bottom. Drawing an annotated tree without the lexval values at the leaves.

What exams ask: Define synthesized and inherited attributes with examples. Write an SDD for a desk calculator and draw the annotated parse tree for an input like 3 * 5 + 4 n. Write an SDD for declarations using inherited attributes and show the dependency graph for int a, b, c. Define S-attributed and L-attributed SDDs and explain their evaluation orders and their relation to bottom-up and top-down parsing.

Recap: An SDD attaches attributes to grammar symbols and semantic rules to productions. Synthesized attributes flow up from children; inherited attributes flow down from the parent and across from left siblings. Dependency graphs define evaluation order through a topological sort. S-attributed SDDs use only synthesized attributes and fit LR parsing; L-attributed SDDs allow left-to-right inherited flow and fit one depth-first pass and top-down parsing. Next lesson we embed actions directly inside productions and use them to build syntax trees.
key_points: An SDD is a grammar plus attributes on symbols and semantic rules on productions.
Synthesized attributes are computed from children (flow up); inherited attributes from parent and siblings (flow down or across).
Desk calculator: E.val = E1.val + T.val, T.val = T1.val * F.val, F.val = digit.lexval; 3 * 5 + 4 gives 19.
In D -> T L, L.inh = T.type passes the declared type down to every identifier in int a, b, c.
A dependency graph orders attribute evaluation; any topological sort works; a cycle means no valid order.
S-attributed: only synthesized attributes; evaluated bottom-up, fits LR parsing and Yacc actions.
L-attributed: inherited attributes depend only on the parent's inherited and left siblings; one left-to-right depth-first pass, fits top-down parsing.
lessons.tip: To classify an attribute, look at the production where its rule is written. If the symbol is on the left side, it is synthesized; if it is on the right side, it is inherited.
lessons.task: Draw the annotated parse tree for ( 2 + 3 ) * 4 n using the desk calculator SDD. Then draw the dependency graph for float x, y using the declaration SDD and give one valid evaluation order.

quiz.q: In E -> E1 + T with rule E.val = E1.val + T.val, E.val is:
quiz.explain: It is computed at the node from its children's values, so it is synthesized.

quiz.q: In D -> T L with rule L.inh = T.type, L.inh is:
options: Inherited, from a sibling through the parent
quiz.explain: L gets its value from its left sibling T via the parent's production, so it is inherited.

quiz.q: What value is printed for 3 * 5 + 4 n with the desk calculator SDD?
quiz.explain: 3 * 5 = 15 is computed first, then 15 + 4 = 19.

quiz.q: Which SDDs fit naturally with LR (bottom-up) parsing?
options: SDDs where inherited attributes depend on right siblings
quiz.explain: With only synthesized attributes, values can be computed at each reduction.

quiz.q: Which rule breaks the L-attributed condition in A -> B C?
quiz.explain: B's inherited attribute depends on C, which is to its right.

lessons.title: Translation Schemes, Syntax Trees and DAGs
lessons.content:
Imagine a wedding cook in Old Dhaka preparing kacchi biriyani from a recipe card. The card does not only list ingredients; it also says when to act: after the meat is marinated, add the potatoes; after the rice is layered, seal the pot with dough. The action is written at a precise point in the sequence. A syntax-directed translation scheme is a recipe card for a grammar: it puts small pieces of code at precise positions inside productions, and they run exactly when the parser reaches those positions.

From SDD to SDT: In the last lesson, an SDD listed semantic rules next to each production without saying when they run. A syntax-directed translation scheme, or SDT, embeds program fragments called semantic actions inside the right side of productions, written in braces, for example E -> E1 + T { print('+') }. The position of the action matters: an action placed between two symbols runs after the symbols to its left have been fully recognised. SDTs are how SDDs are implemented in practice, whether in hand-written parsers or in Yacc.

Postfix SDTs: The simplest and most common case is when all actions are at the right end of productions. Such an SDT is called postfix. Any S-attributed SDD can be turned into a postfix SDT by writing each rule as an action at the end of its production. In a bottom-up parser, the action runs at the moment of reduction, which is exactly what Yacc does with its actions.

Postfix SDTs on the LR stack: An LR parser can keep attribute values on its stack, next to the states. When it reduces by E -> E1 + T, the values of E1, + and T are the top three entries. The action computes the sum, the three entries are popped, and the new E entry, holding the sum, is pushed. In code-like form: stack[top - 2].val = stack[top - 2].val + stack[top].val; top = top - 2. This is precisely what $$ = $1 + $3 does behind the scenes in Yacc.

Infix to postfix translation: A classic SDT translates arithmetic in infix form into postfix form, where operators follow their operands. Scheme: expr -> expr + term { print('+') } | expr - term { print('-') } | term; term -> 0 { print('0') } | 1 { print('1') } and so on up to 9. For the input 9 - 5 + 2, the parser recognises 9 and prints 9, recognises 5 and prints 5, reduces expr - term and prints -, recognises 2 and prints 2, reduces expr + term and prints +. The output is 9 5 - 2 +, which is correct postfix. Postfix form needs no brackets and is easy for a stack machine to evaluate.

Actions in the middle: Sometimes an action must run in the middle of a production, for instance to pass an inherited attribute down before a symbol is parsed. In B -> X { a } Y, action a runs after X has been recognised and before Y is processed. The rule for implementing an L-attributed SDD as an SDT is: put an action that computes an inherited attribute of a symbol immediately before that symbol, and put actions that compute synthesized attributes of the head at the end of the production.

Middle actions in top-down parsing: In recursive descent, a middle action is simply code written at that point in the function for B: call X(), run a, call Y(). Inherited attributes become function parameters and synthesized attributes become return values. For example, the function for T' from lesson 15 takes the running product inh as a parameter, multiplies by F's value and passes the result to the recursive call, and returns the final value. L-attributed SDTs and recursive descent fit together naturally.

Middle actions in bottom-up parsing: An LR parser only runs code on reductions, so a middle action needs a trick. We introduce a new marker nonterminal M with production M -> ε and attach the action to it: B -> X M Y, M -> ε { a }. When the parser has X on the stack and is about to process Y, it reduces ε to M, running a. Yacc does this automatically when you write an action in the middle of a rule. The markers can sometimes introduce new conflicts, which is one reason Yacc warns about mid-rule actions.

Parse trees vs abstract syntax trees: A parse tree records every step of the derivation, including chain productions like E -> T -> F, brackets and punctuation. An abstract syntax tree, or AST, keeps only what matters for meaning. Each interior node is an operator or construct, and its children are its operands or components. For a - 4 + c, the AST has + at the root, with children a - 4 subtree and c; the - node has children a and 4. No E, T or F nodes, and no brackets, because the tree shape already shows grouping. Most compilers build an AST and use it for type checking and code generation.

Building an AST with an SDD: We use two constructors: Leaf(op, val) makes a leaf node, and Node(op, c1, c2, ...) makes an interior node. Rules: E -> E1 + T has E.node = new Node('+', E1.node, T.node). E -> E1 - T has E.node = new Node('-', E1.node, T.node). E -> T has E.node = T.node. T -> ( E ) has T.node = E.node. T -> id has T.node = new Leaf(id, id.entry). T -> num has T.node = new Leaf(num, num.val). The definition is S-attributed, so a bottom-up parser builds the tree during reductions.

Tracing a - 4 + c: The parser reduces a first, creating p1 = Leaf(id, entry for a). Then 4 gives p2 = Leaf(num, 4). Reducing E - T gives p3 = Node('-', p1, p2). Then c gives p4 = Leaf(id, entry for c). Reducing E + T gives p5 = Node('+', p3, p4). The pointer p5 is the root of the AST. Five nodes, built in exactly the order of the reductions.

The same AST from a top-down parser: With the left-recursion-free grammar E -> T E', E' -> + T E' | - T E' | ε, we use inherited attributes: E' receives the tree built so far as inh, adds a new node with the next operand, and passes the bigger tree down, returning the final tree as syn. For a - 4 + c, E' first receives the leaf a, builds Node('-', a, 4), passes it down, then builds Node('+', that node, c). The resulting AST is the same as the bottom-up one, with correct left associativity. This is the practical payoff of inherited attributes.

Directed acyclic graphs: In an expression, the same subexpression often appears more than once. A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, for an expression is like an AST, but a node for a common subexpression is created only once and shared. For a + a * ( b - c ) + ( b - c ) * d, the AST has two separate leaves for a and two separate subtrees for b - c. In the DAG, there is one leaf a with two parents, and one b - c node with two parents. The DAG directly tells the compiler that b - c needs to be computed only once.

Building DAGs: The same SDD that builds ASTs can build DAGs, with one change: before creating a node, the constructors check whether an identical node already exists, with the same operator and the same children. If it does, they return the existing node instead of creating a new one. So the second call to Node('-', b, c) returns the node made by the first call.

The value-number method: To make this check fast, nodes are stored in an array, and each node is referred to by its index, called its value number. Each interior node is identified by a signature, the triple of its operator, left child number and right child number. A hash table maps signatures to value numbers. For i = i + 10: entry 1 is the leaf id pointing to i; entry 2 is the leaf num 10; entry 3 is + with children 1 and 2; entry 4 is = with children 1 and 3. If the program later computes i + 10 again, the lookup of the signature +, 1, 2 finds entry 3 instead of creating a new node. Lesson 24 uses DAGs exactly like this to eliminate common subexpressions inside a basic block.

Real life example 1, Excel formula recalculation: When you type =B1*C1 + B1*C1 in a spreadsheet, the program parses the formula into a tree. A smart spreadsheet engine can notice that B1*C1 occurs twice and compute it once, like a DAG. Spreadsheets also keep a dependency graph between cells, very similar to attribute dependency graphs, so that changing one cell recomputes only the cells that depend on it.

Real life example 2, a Bangla calculator app for shopkeepers: A developer in Rajshahi builds a calculator app for shopkeepers that accepts expressions with Bangla digits. The app's parser builds an AST from the input, then walks the tree to compute the result and also to show the calculation steps in words, such as first multiply, then add. One tree, two translations, both written as small actions attached to grammar rules.

Common mistakes: Placing an action that computes an inherited attribute after the symbol that needs it. Forgetting that postfix SDT actions run on reduction, so printing order follows reduction order, not reading order. Building an AST with nodes for every nonterminal, which turns it back into a parse tree. In DAGs, sharing nodes that only look similar but have different operators or different children. Forgetting that for 9 - 5 + 2 the correct postfix is 9 5 - 2 +, not 9 5 2 + -.

What exams ask: Define a syntax-directed translation scheme and explain how it differs from an SDD. Write an SDT that translates infix expressions into postfix and show the output for a given input. Construct a syntax tree for an expression like a - 4 + c using node constructors, listing the steps. Construct the DAG for an expression such as a + a * ( b - c ) + ( b - c ) * d and explain the value-number method.

Recap: An SDT embeds actions inside productions; their position decides when they run. Postfix SDTs, with actions at the end, run on LR reductions and are what Yacc implements. Middle actions suit recursive descent directly and need marker nonterminals in LR parsing. An abstract syntax tree keeps only operators and operands, built with Leaf and Node constructors. A DAG shares identical subexpressions, built with the value-number method and a hash table. Next lesson we use these trees to check types.
key_points: An SDT puts semantic actions in braces inside productions; an action runs after the symbols to its left are recognised.
Postfix SDTs (actions at the end) run on LR reductions; S-attributed SDDs become postfix SDTs.
Infix-to-postfix SDT: 9 - 5 + 2 is translated to 9 5 - 2 +.
Put actions computing inherited attributes just before the symbol; in LR parsing use marker nonterminals M -> ε.
An abstract syntax tree has operators as interior nodes and operands as children, without chain productions or brackets.
Leaf and Node constructors build the AST of a - 4 + c in five steps: p1 to p5.
A DAG shares identical subexpressions; the value-number method looks up (op, left, right) signatures in a hash table.
lessons.tip: When asked to build an AST or DAG, first list the node-creation steps p1, p2, ... in order, then draw. The list makes sharing in a DAG obvious and earns the marks.
lessons.task: Write the postfix translation of ( 8 - 3 ) * 2 + 7 by hand using the SDT idea. Then draw both the AST and the DAG for x * y + x * y - z and list the value-number table for the DAG.

quiz.q: What is the output of the infix-to-postfix SDT for 9 - 5 + 2?
quiz.explain: 9 and 5 are printed, then - on reduction, then 2, then + on the final reduction.

quiz.q: In B -> X { a } Y, when does action a run?
options: After X is recognised and before Y is processed
quiz.explain: An embedded action runs after all symbols to its left have been recognised.

quiz.q: How does an LR parser handle an action in the middle of a production?
options: It runs it at the start of parsing
It uses a marker nonterminal M -> ε that carries the action
quiz.explain: Reducing the empty marker at the right moment executes the action.

quiz.q: Which statement about an abstract syntax tree is true?
options: It contains a node for every grammar symbol
Interior nodes are operators and children are operands
It always has more nodes than the parse tree
quiz.explain: An AST drops chain productions and punctuation, keeping operators and operands.

quiz.q: In a DAG for a + a * ( b - c ) + ( b - c ) * d, how many nodes represent b - c?
quiz.explain: A DAG creates the common subexpression once and lets both uses point to it.

lessons.title: Type Checking
lessons.content:
Think of a fuel station on the Dhaka-Chattogram highway. A diesel truck must not get octane, and a motorbike must not get diesel. A careful attendant checks the vehicle type before filling, because a mismatch damages the engine. In a program, every value also has a type, such as integer, float, character or pointer, and operations only make sense for certain types. Adding two numbers is fine; multiplying a string by a function is nonsense. The type checker is the careful attendant of the compiler: it makes sure every operation gets operands of the right type before the program ever runs.

What type checking is: Type checking is the part of semantic analysis that verifies that the types of all constructs in a program follow the rules of the language. It also computes the type of each expression, which later phases need: the code for adding two integers is different from the code for adding two floats, and the size of a variable depends on its type. When the rules are broken, the type checker reports a type error, such as incompatible types in assignment or array index is not an integer.

Why it matters: Type errors are among the most common programming mistakes. Catching them at compile time saves debugging time and prevents crashes in front of users. Types also let the compiler choose the right machine instructions, allocate the right amount of memory and perform optimizations safely. Finally, type information documents the program: reading a function signature tells you what it expects and returns.

Type expressions: To reason about types, compilers represent them as type expressions. Basic types are type expressions: boolean, char, integer, float and void. Type constructors build bigger types from smaller ones. array(n, T) is an array of n elements of type T. pointer(T) is a pointer to T. A record or struct type lists field names with their types. s × t is a pair, the Cartesian product, used for function argument lists. s -> t is a function from s to t. For example, the C declaration int a[2][3] has the type expression array(2, array(3, integer)), and a function int f(char, float) has type char × float -> integer.

Type systems: A type system is the collection of rules that assign type expressions to the parts of a program. The type checker implements a type system, often as an SDT over the syntax tree. A type system is called sound if, whenever it accepts a program, that program cannot have type errors at run time. A language is strongly typed if its compiler can guarantee that accepted programs will run without type errors. Java is usually described as strongly typed. C is often called weakly typed because it allows things like casting any pointer to any other pointer, which can lead to type errors that the compiler cannot see.

Static and dynamic checking: Static type checking happens at compile time, using declarations and inference. Dynamic type checking happens at run time, by storing a type tag with each value and checking it before each operation. C, C++, Java, Go and Rust are mainly statically checked. Python and JavaScript are dynamically checked: x = 5 then x = 'hello' is fine, and an error such as adding a number to a list appears only when that line runs. Some checks must be dynamic even in static languages, such as array bounds checking in Java, because the index is only known at run time.

Type synthesis and type inference: Type synthesis builds the type of an expression from the types of its parts, which must already be known; for example, if f has type s -> t and x has type s, then f(x) has type t. This is what C and Java mainly do, using declared types. Type inference works out types from how names are used, even when they are not declared. Languages like Haskell and ML infer types for whole programs, and modern languages offer local inference, such as var in Java and auto in C++, where the type of a variable is taken from its initial value.

Rules for expressions: Using the syntax tree or an SDT, we give a rule for each construct. Literals: a number like 42 has type integer, 3.5 has type float. Identifiers: look up the declared type in the symbol table. Arithmetic E -> E1 + E2: if both operands are integer, the result is integer; if both are float, the result is float; if one is integer and one float, convert the integer to float and the result is float; otherwise report a type error. Comparisons such as E1 < E2 require comparable operands and produce boolean.

Rules for arrays, pointers and functions: Array access E -> E1 [ E2 ]: if E1 has type array(n, t) and E2 has type integer, then E has type t; otherwise error. So if a has type array(2, array(3, integer)), then a[i] has type array(3, integer) and a[i][j] has type integer. Pointer dereference E -> * E1: if E1 has type pointer(t), then E has type t. Function call E -> E1 ( E2 ): if E1 has type s -> t and E2 has type s, then E has type t. These rules turn directly into code that walks the tree.

Rules for statements: Statements do not produce values, so we give them type void when they are correct and type_error otherwise. Assignment S -> id = E: if id and E have the same type, or E can be converted to id's type, S is void. If-statement S -> if ( E ) S1: E must have type boolean, and S1 must be void. While-statement S -> while ( E ) S1: the same condition. A sequence of statements is void only if every statement is void. In C, conditions are integers rather than booleans, so the rule there checks for a scalar type instead.

Coercions: Many languages convert types automatically in mixed expressions. In Java, the widening order for numbers is byte, short, int, long, float, double, with char also widening to int. A widening conversion moves up this order and is done implicitly, because no information is lost in the usual case. A narrowing conversion, such as double to int, can lose information, so it requires an explicit cast like (int) x. Conversions done automatically by the compiler are called coercions or implicit conversions; conversions written by the programmer are explicit conversions or casts.

How coercion appears in code: For position = initial + rate * 60, the type checker sees float * integer, decides that the integer must be widened to float, and inserts a conversion node. In three-address code this becomes t1 = inttofloat(60), as you saw in lesson 2. A compiler typically uses two helper functions: max(t1, t2) returns the wider of two types in the hierarchy, and widen(a, t, w) generates the conversion of address a from type t to wider type w if they differ. Some constant conversions are done at compile time, so 60 can simply become 60.0.

Type equivalence: When are two types the same? Under structural equivalence, two types are the same if they are the same basic type or are built by the same constructor from equivalent types; names do not matter. Under name equivalence, each declared type name is a distinct type, so two variables are compatible only if they are declared with the same type name. For example, if you declare type Taka = integer and type Marks = integer, structural equivalence treats Taka and Marks as the same, while strict name equivalence treats them as different, which can stop you from adding money to exam marks by mistake. C uses structural equivalence for most types but treats each struct declaration as a new, distinct type, even if two structs have identical fields.

Overloading: A symbol is overloaded if it has different meanings depending on context. In most languages + adds integers and also floats, and in Java it also concatenates strings. Java and C++ also allow overloaded functions: several methods called print with different parameter types. The type checker resolves overloading by looking at the argument types and picking the matching definition; if none or more than one matches, it reports an error.

Polymorphism: A polymorphic function can work with arguments of many types. A function length that counts the elements of a list does not care what the elements are. Its type can be written as for all α, list(α) -> integer, where α is a type variable. This is parametric polymorphism, provided by generics in Java and C# and templates in C++. Checking polymorphic code requires matching type expressions with variables, called unification, which is the heart of type inference in languages like ML; details are beyond this course.

Real life example 1, TypeScript in a Bangladeshi startup: A team in Dhaka maintains a large JavaScript web app for an e-commerce site. Bugs keep appearing where a price arrives as the string '500' and gets concatenated instead of added, showing 5005 instead of 505. They switch to TypeScript, which adds static type checking to JavaScript. Now the compiler reports that a string cannot be passed where a number is expected, catching these bugs before customers see them.

Real life example 2, NID and phone numbers: A form stores a phone number such as 01712345678. If it is treated as an integer, the leading zero disappears and arithmetic like adding 1 becomes possible, which makes no sense for a phone number. A well-typed system declares it as a string or a special PhoneNumber type, so the compiler or validator rejects arithmetic on it. Choosing types carefully, and letting the type checker enforce them, prevents real data bugs.

Common mistakes: Confusing strong typing with static typing; Python is dynamically but fairly strongly typed. Saying widening needs a cast; it is implicit, narrowing needs a cast. Writing array(3, array(2, integer)) for int a[2][3], with the dimensions reversed. Forgetting that statements get type void, not the type of their expression. Thinking type checking is part of parsing; it is semantic analysis, done on the tree.

What exams ask: Define type expressions and write them for given declarations. Distinguish static and dynamic checking, strong and weak typing. Write type checking rules or an SDT for expressions, arrays, functions and statements. Explain coercion with the widening hierarchy and show how inttofloat is inserted. Explain structural versus name equivalence with an example. Short notes on overloading and polymorphic functions.

Recap: Type checking verifies that every operation gets operands of acceptable types and computes types for later phases. Types are written as type expressions built from basic types and constructors such as array, pointer and ->. Static checking happens at compile time, dynamic checking at run time; a sound type system guarantees no run-time type errors. Rules for expressions, arrays, functions and statements are applied over the syntax tree; widening is implicit and inserts conversions, narrowing needs a cast. Next lesson we choose an intermediate representation to translate the checked program into.
key_points: Type checking verifies operand types follow the language rules and computes each expression's type.
Type expressions: basic types plus constructors array(n, T), pointer(T), records, products s × t and functions s -> t.
int a[2][3] has type array(2, array(3, integer)); a[i] has type array(3, integer).
Static checking is at compile time, dynamic at run time; a sound type system rules out run-time type errors.
Rules: E1 + E2 gives integer or float (with conversion); E1[E2] needs an integer index; f(x) needs x to match the parameter type; statements get type void.
Widening (int to float) is implicit and inserts inttofloat; narrowing (double to int) needs an explicit cast.
Structural equivalence compares type structure; name equivalence compares declared type names.
lessons.tip: For every new construct you meet, write its type rule in the form: if the parts have types X and Y, then the whole has type Z, otherwise type_error. Exam answers in this form are short and score well.
lessons.task: Write type expressions for: char name[20]; float *p; int add(int, int); and a struct with an int roll and float cgpa. Then write the type rules a checker would apply to p[3] + add(2, 3) and say which conversion is inserted.

quiz.q: What is the type expression for the C declaration int a[2][3]?
quiz.explain: a is an array of 2 elements, each an array of 3 integers.

quiz.q: If f has type char × float -> integer and the call is f(c, x) with c a char and x a float, the call has type:
quiz.explain: Arguments match the parameter type, so the result is the function's return type.

quiz.q: Which conversion normally requires an explicit cast in Java?
quiz.explain: Narrowing conversions can lose information, so Java requires a cast.

quiz.q: A type system is called sound when:
options: Accepted programs cannot have type errors at run time
It checks types only at run time
quiz.explain: Soundness means the static checks guarantee no run-time type errors.

quiz.q: Under strict name equivalence, types Taka = integer and Marks = integer are:
quiz.explain: Each declared name is a distinct type under name equivalence, even with the same structure.

lessons.title: Intermediate Representations and Three-Address Code
lessons.content:
Imagine the United Nations in New York with speakers of 6 official languages. If every pair of languages needed its own translator, 6 languages would need 30 one-way translators. Instead, many meetings use relay interpretation: a speech is first rendered into a common language, and from there into the others. Compilers use the same trick. Instead of translating each source language straight into each machine language, they translate into a common middle language, the intermediate representation, and translate from there to each machine.

What an IR is: An intermediate representation, or IR, is the form a program takes inside the compiler between the source code and the target code. The front end produces it after parsing and type checking. The optimizer improves it. The back end turns it into machine code. A good IR is easy to produce from the source, easy to translate to real machines, and easy to analyse and transform. No single form is best at everything, so many compilers use more than one IR at different stages.

Why we need it: First, retargeting: with m languages and n machines, a common IR needs only m front ends and n back ends instead of m times n compilers, as we saw in lesson 2. Second, optimization: many improvements, like removing repeated calculations or moving work out of loops, do not depend on the target machine. Doing them once on the IR helps every language and every machine. Third, simplicity: each phase deals with a smaller problem.

High-level and low-level IRs: IRs range from high level to low level. A high-level IR, such as an abstract syntax tree, stays close to the source: loops, array indexing and function calls are still visible. That suits type checking and some loop optimizations. A low-level IR is close to machine code: explicit address calculations, jumps and temporaries. That suits register allocation and instruction selection. Three-address code sits in the middle and is the most common IR taught and used.

Syntax trees and DAGs: From lessons 16 and 17 you already know two graphical IRs. The syntax tree shows structure; the DAG also shares common subexpressions, telling the compiler which values can be computed once. For a = b * -c + b * -c, the tree has two copies of the b * -c subtree, while the DAG has just one, used twice.

Postfix notation: Postfix, also called reverse Polish notation, writes operators after their operands. a + b * c becomes a b c * +. ( a + b ) * c becomes a b + c *. It needs no brackets and can be evaluated with a single stack: push operands, and for each operator pop its operands and push the result. Stack-based virtual machines, such as the Java Virtual Machine, use instructions very close to postfix form: iload a, iload b, iadd.

Three-address code: In three-address code, each instruction has at most one operator on the right side, and at most three addresses: two operands and one result. A source expression like x + y * z is broken into t1 = y * z; t2 = x + t1, where t1 and t2 are compiler-generated temporaries. An address can be a name from the source, a constant, or a temporary. Because everything is spelled out in small steps, the evaluation order is explicit, which makes optimization and code generation easier.

The instruction forms: The common forms are: assignment with a binary operator, x = y op z; with a unary operator, x = op y, such as minus or a conversion like inttofloat; copy, x = y; unconditional jump, goto L; conditional jumps, if x goto L, ifFalse x goto L and if x relop y goto L; procedure calls, param x for each argument followed by call p, n or y = call p, n, where n is the number of arguments, and return y; indexed copies, x = y[i] and x[i] = y; and address and pointer operations, x = &y, x = *y and *x = y. Labels mark jump targets.

Where temporaries come from: The compiler creates a fresh temporary name, t1, t2, t3 and so on, every time it needs to hold an intermediate value. At this stage it does not worry about how many there are; a program might use hundreds. Later, the register allocator decides which temporaries share the same register and which must live in memory. Keeping the IR free from these machine limits is exactly what makes it easy to generate and to optimize.

A loop example: The C statement do i = i + 1; while ( a[i] < v ); with 8-byte array elements can be translated as: L: t1 = i + 1; i = t1; t2 = i * 8; t3 = a [ t2 ]; if t3 < v goto L. The loop becomes straight-line code plus a conditional jump back to the label. The index is multiplied by the element size to get a byte offset, a detail the source code hides but the IR must show.

The running example: Take a = b * -c + b * -c. Its three-address code, made from the syntax tree, is: t1 = minus c; t2 = b * t1; t3 = minus c; t4 = b * t3; t5 = t2 + t4; a = t5. Six instructions. From the DAG we could produce the shorter t1 = minus c; t2 = b * t1; t5 = t2 + t2; a = t5. Three-address code is an abstract form; we now look at three concrete ways to store it.

Quadruples: A quadruple has four fields: op, arg1, arg2 and result. Our example becomes: 0: minus, c, blank, t1. 1: *, b, t1, t2. 2: minus, c, blank, t3. 3: *, b, t3, t4. 4: +, t2, t4, t5. 5: =, t5, blank, a. Unary operators and copies leave arg2 empty; jumps put the target label in result. Quadruples name every temporary explicitly, so the temporaries need symbol table entries, but instructions can be moved around freely during optimization because references are by name.

Triples: A triple has only three fields: op, arg1 and arg2. Instead of naming a temporary, the result of an instruction is referred to by its position. Our example: 0: minus, c. 1: *, b, (0). 2: minus, c. 3: *, b, (2). 4: +, (1), (3). 5: =, a, (4). Here (0) means the value computed by triple 0. Triples save space and do not need temporaries in the symbol table. But if the optimizer moves an instruction, every reference to its position must be updated. An operation like x[i] = y needs two triples, one to compute the address and one to store.

Indirect triples: Indirect triples add a separate list of pointers to triples, which defines the order of execution. For example, the instruction list might say 35: (0), 36: (1), 37: (2) and so on. To reorder the program, the optimizer reorders the pointer list and leaves the triples themselves untouched. This gives the space saving of triples with the flexibility of quadruples, at the cost of one more level of indirection.

Comparing the three: Quadruples are the simplest to manipulate and the most common in teaching and in many compilers, but they use the most space. Triples are compact but awkward to rearrange. Indirect triples are compact and rearrangeable, but slightly more complex. Exam questions often ask you to write the same code in all three forms, so practise writing them side by side.

Static single assignment form: SSA is an IR where every variable is assigned exactly once. Each new assignment to a source variable creates a new version: p = a + b; q = p - c; p = q * d becomes p1 = a + b; q1 = p1 - c; p2 = q1 * d. Now each use clearly refers to one definition, which makes many optimizations simpler. Where control flow merges, SSA uses a φ (phi) function: if ( flag ) x = -1; else x = 1; y = x * a; becomes x1 = -1 in one branch, x2 = 1 in the other, then x3 = φ(x1, x2); y = x3 * a, meaning x3 takes x1 or x2 depending on which branch was taken. LLVM's IR is in SSA form, and so is the main IR used inside GCC's optimizer.

Real IRs in the world: Java bytecode is a stack-based IR, stored in .class files and run by the JVM. LLVM IR is a typed, SSA-based, three-address-style IR used by Clang, Rust, Swift and many other compilers; you can see it by asking Clang to emit LLVM code for a small C file. Microsoft's .NET uses a stack-based bytecode called CIL. WebAssembly is a portable, stack-based instruction format that browsers compile to machine code. All of these are IRs in the sense of this lesson.

Real life example 1, building an app for both Android and iPhone: A Bangladeshi startup writes its mobile app in a cross-platform framework. Their code is compiled into an intermediate form and then into ARM machine code for phones, or into JavaScript for the web. One front end, several back ends. Without an IR, they would need a separate compiler for each platform.

Real life example 2, a recipe translated for different kitchens: A Bangladeshi cookbook writer first writes a recipe as clear numbered steps with exact amounts: step 1, heat 2 tablespoons of oil; step 2, add one sliced onion. From that one standard version, editors can adapt it to a gas stove, an electric cooker or a clay oven. The numbered steps are like three-address code: small, explicit, one operation each, and easy to adapt to any kitchen.

Common mistakes: Putting two operators in one three-address instruction, such as t1 = a + b * c. Forgetting that triples refer to earlier results by position, not by temporary names. Confusing the order of fields in quadruples; it is op, arg1, arg2, result. Forgetting to multiply the index by the element width in array accesses. Thinking SSA means a variable can never change at run time; it means each name is assigned in only one place in the program text.

What exams ask: Explain why intermediate code is used and list its advantages. Translate an expression such as a = b * -c + b * -c or a statement with arrays into three-address code. Represent it as quadruples, triples and indirect triples and compare these forms. Convert an expression into postfix notation. Short notes on SSA form and φ functions.

Recap: An IR is the compiler's internal middle language, enabling retargeting, machine-independent optimization and simpler phases. Graphical IRs include syntax trees and DAGs; linear IRs include postfix and three-address code. Three-address code uses instructions with at most one operator and three addresses, stored as quadruples (op, arg1, arg2, result), triples (op, arg1, arg2 with positional references) or indirect triples. SSA gives each variable a single assignment and uses φ at merges. Next lesson we generate three-address code for declarations, expressions and arrays.
key_points: An IR sits between source and target, enabling retargeting (m + n instead of m x n) and machine-independent optimization.
Graphical IRs: syntax trees and DAGs; linear IRs: postfix and three-address code.
Three-address code has at most one operator per instruction: x = y op z, x = op y, x = y, goto L, if x relop y goto L, param, call, x = y[i], x = *y.
a = b * -c + b * -c becomes t1 = minus c; t2 = b * t1; t3 = minus c; t4 = b * t3; t5 = t2 + t4; a = t5.
Quadruples store op, arg1, arg2, result; triples store op, arg1, arg2 and refer to results by position.
Indirect triples add a list of pointers so instructions can be reordered without changing the triples.
SSA assigns each variable once and uses φ functions where control flow merges; LLVM IR is in SSA form.
lessons.tip: When asked for quadruples, triples and indirect triples, write the three-address code first, then fill the three tables row by row from it. It is mechanical once the code is right.
lessons.task: Write three-address code for x = ( a + b ) * ( a + b ) - c / d. Then write it as quadruples, triples and indirect triples (start the pointer list at 50). Finally, write the shorter version you could get from the DAG.

quiz.q: Which is a valid three-address instruction?
quiz.explain: Three-address code allows at most one operator on the right side.

quiz.q: What is the postfix form of ( a + b ) * c?
quiz.explain: a b + computes a + b, then c is pushed and * multiplies.

quiz.q: In triples, how is the result of an earlier instruction referred to?
options: By a temporary name like t1
quiz.explain: Triples have no result field; later triples point to earlier ones by position.

quiz.q: What advantage do indirect triples have over triples?
options: Instructions can be reordered by changing a pointer list only
quiz.explain: The optimizer reorders the pointer list, leaving the triples and their references intact.

quiz.q: In SSA form, what does x3 = φ(x1, x2) mean?
options: x3 is the sum of x1 and x2
x3 takes the value of x1 or x2 depending on which path reached this point
x3 is a pointer to x1
quiz.explain: A φ function merges versions of a variable from different control-flow paths.

lessons.title: Translating Declarations, Expressions and Arrays
lessons.content:
Imagine a new apartment building in Uttara where the manager assigns flats. The first family takes flat 0 and needs 4 rooms, so the next family starts at room 4. A bigger family needs 8 rooms and starts at 4, so the following one starts at 12. A family renting a block of 10 small units of 4 rooms each takes 40 rooms starting at 12. At the end, the manager knows exactly where every family lives just by keeping a running counter. A compiler lays out variables in memory in exactly this way, then uses those positions to generate three-address code for expressions and array accesses.

What this lesson does: We now produce intermediate code. First, declarations: for each variable, decide its type, its size in bytes, called its width, and its position, called its relative address or offset. Second, expressions and assignments: emit three-address instructions that compute values in temporaries. Third, arrays: compute the address of an element like a[i][j] from the base address and the indexes. All of this is written as syntax-directed translation, building on the last four lessons.

Widths of types: The amount of storage a type needs is its width. On a typical target, we can assume char has width 1, integer width 4 and float width 8; the exact numbers depend on the machine, so compilers keep them in a table. An array of n elements of type t has width n times the width of t. So int[10] has width 40 and int[2][3], which is array(2, array(3, integer)), has width 2 times 12 = 24. A record has the sum of its fields' widths, plus any padding.

Alignment: Real processors often require or prefer that a value of width 4 or 8 starts at an address that is a multiple of 4 or 8. So the compiler may leave small unused gaps, called padding, between variables or struct fields. For example, a struct with a char followed by an int often has width 8, not 5, because 3 bytes of padding are inserted after the char. Exam problems usually ignore alignment unless they say otherwise.

The declaration SDT: A global variable offset starts at 0. For each declaration D -> T id ;, the action stores the name in the symbol table with its type and the current offset, then increases offset by the type's width: top.put(id.lexeme, T.type, offset); offset = offset + T.width. Types are built by B -> int, which sets type integer and width 4, B -> float, which sets type float and width 8, and C -> [ num ] C1, which sets C.type = array(num.value, C1.type) and C.width = num.value times C1.width. The base type and width are passed down to C as inherited attributes.

Tracing a declaration list: For int a; float b; int c[10]; offset starts at 0. a gets type integer, offset 0, and offset becomes 4. b gets type float, offset 4, and offset becomes 12. c gets type array(10, integer), offset 12, width 40, and offset becomes 52. The procedure needs 52 bytes for these locals. These offsets are relative: at run time they are added to the address of the data area, as lesson 21 will explain.

Nested scopes: In C, Java and most languages, blocks can declare their own variables, and an inner declaration can hide an outer one. Compilers handle this with one symbol table per scope, each with a pointer to the table of the enclosing scope. Entering a block creates a new table; leaving it discards or saves the table. A lookup searches the current table first, then follows the chain outward. So in { int x; { float x; x = 1.5; } x = 2; }, the inner assignment finds the float x and the outer one finds the int x.

Translating expressions: We give each expression E an attribute E.addr, the address holding its value: a name, a constant or a temporary. The function gen emits one three-address instruction. Rules: E -> E1 + E2: E.addr = new Temp(); gen(E.addr = E1.addr + E2.addr). E -> - E1: E.addr = new Temp(); gen(E.addr = minus E1.addr). E -> ( E1 ): E.addr = E1.addr, no code. E -> id: E.addr = the symbol table entry of id, no code. And for assignment S -> id = E: gen(id = E.addr). Each operator produces exactly one instruction.

Tracing an assignment: For a = b + - c: E -> id gives b and c their own names. E -> - E1 creates t1 and emits t1 = minus c. E -> E1 + E2 creates t2 and emits t2 = b + t1. Finally the assignment emits a = t2. The code is t1 = minus c; t2 = b + t1; a = t2. This style is called incremental translation: instructions are emitted into one growing array as the parser goes. An older style builds a code attribute, E.code, by concatenating the code of the children; it gives the same result but copies strings around.

One-dimensional arrays: If array A starts at address base and each element has width w, and indexes start at 0, then A[i] is at base + i times w. For an int array with base 1000 and w = 4, A[5] is at 1000 + 20 = 1020. If indexes start at some lower bound low, as in Pascal, the address is base + (i - low) times w, which can be rewritten as i times w + (base - low times w). The bracketed part is known at compile time and can be computed once, so at run time only i times w and one addition are needed.

Two-dimensional arrays, row-major: A two-dimensional array is stored in one long line of memory. In row-major order, used by C, C++ and Java arrays, row 0 is stored first, then row 1, and so on. For A with n2 columns, element A[i1][i2] is at base + ( i1 times n2 + i2 ) times w. Equivalently base + i1 times w1 + i2 times w2, where w2 = w is the element width and w1 = n2 times w is the width of a whole row. For int M[3][4] with base 1000, M[2][1] is at 1000 + ( 2 times 4 + 1 ) times 4 = 1000 + 36 = 1036.

Column-major order: Fortran, MATLAB and some others store arrays column by column. Then A[i1][i2] in an array with n1 rows is at base + ( i2 times n1 + i1 ) times w. For the same M[3][4] stored column-major, M[2][1] is at 1000 + ( 1 times 3 + 2 ) times 4 = 1020. The same element lives at different addresses depending on the layout, which matters when C code calls Fortran libraries or when you want cache-friendly loops.

Higher dimensions: The same idea extends to any number of dimensions. For a three-dimensional row-major array with sizes n1, n2 and n3, element A[i1][i2][i3] is at base + ( ( i1 times n2 + i2 ) times n3 + i3 ) times w. Each index is multiplied by the product of the sizes of all the dimensions to its right. The compiler builds this sum one index at a time, which is why the translation scheme walks down the list of indexes, multiplying and adding as it goes.

Three-address code for array references: The translation computes the offset step by step and then uses an indexed copy. Take c + a[i][j], where a is int[2][3], so the element width is 4 and a row has width 12. The code is: t1 = i * 12; t2 = j * 4; t3 = t1 + t2; t4 = a [ t3 ]; t5 = c + t4. The SDT uses an attribute L.type to know the current element type and its width as it walks down the index list, and L.addr to accumulate the offset. Assigning into an array, like a[i] = x, uses the other indexed form: t1 = i * 4; a [ t1 ] = x.

Type conversions in code: Mixed types need explicit conversion instructions. For x = a + i where a is float and i is int, the type checker computes max(float, integer) = float and the translation calls widen on i, giving: t1 = inttofloat i; t2 = a + t1; x = t2. If both operands already have the result type, widen returns the address unchanged and no extra instruction is emitted. Narrowing assignments, like assigning a float to an int variable in C, would produce a conversion such as floattoint in the opposite direction.

Real life example 1, exam seat plans: A university in Sylhet stores exam hall seat plans as a two-dimensional table of rows and columns. A program that finds the student at row 7, column 12 uses exactly the row-major formula: start of the table plus (7 times number of columns plus 12) times the size of one record. When the table has 30 columns and each record takes 64 bytes, the offset is (7 times 30 + 12) times 64 = 14208 bytes from the start.

Real life example 2, image editing apps: A photo on your phone is a two-dimensional array of pixels, often stored row by row with 4 bytes per pixel. A filter that brightens the photo walks over the array using the address formula for every pixel. Compilers turn the source code a[y][x] into exactly the multiply-and-add sequence of this lesson, and then optimize it so that walking along a row just adds 4 each time.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the index by the element width. Using the number of rows instead of the number of columns in the row-major formula. Mixing up base + i times w with base + i when the element width is not 1. Forgetting that offsets increase by width after each declaration, not by 1. Emitting code for E -> ( E1 ), which needs none. And forgetting the conversion instruction in mixed-type expressions.

What exams ask: Write an SDT that computes types, widths and offsets for declarations and trace it on a list like int a; float b; int c[10]. Translate an assignment such as a = b * - c + d into three-address code using the SDT. Derive and apply the address formula for one- and two-dimensional arrays in row-major and column-major order. Generate three-address code for expressions with array references like c + a[i][j].

Recap: Declarations assign each variable a type, a width and a relative offset, using a running offset counter, with one symbol table per scope chained outward. Expressions get an address attribute, and each operator emits one instruction into a temporary. A[i] is at base + i times w; row-major A[i1][i2] is at base + ( i1 times n2 + i2 ) times w, and column-major swaps the roles. Mixed types insert conversion instructions. Next lesson we translate boolean expressions and control flow using jumps and backpatching.
key_points: Each type has a width (e.g. char 1, int 4, float 8); an array's width is the number of elements times the element width.
A running offset gives each declared variable a relative address: int a; float b; int c[10] gives offsets 0, 4, 12 and total 52.
Nested scopes use one symbol table per block chained to the enclosing one; lookup searches outward.
Expressions get E.addr; each operator emits one instruction into a new temporary: a = b + - c gives t1 = minus c; t2 = b + t1; a = t2.
A[i] is at base + i × w; with a lower bound, base + (i - low) × w, with the constant part precomputed.
Row-major A[i1][i2] = base + (i1 × n2 + i2) × w; column-major = base + (i2 × n1 + i1) × w.
For c + a[i][j] with int a[2][3]: t1 = i * 12; t2 = j * 4; t3 = t1 + t2; t4 = a[t3]; t5 = c + t4.
lessons.tip: For any array address question, first write the row width and element width as numbers, then plug in. Most mistakes come from confusing number of rows with number of columns.
lessons.task: For float m[5][6] with base address 2000 and float width 8, compute the address of m[3][4] in row-major and in column-major order. Then write three-address code for x = m[i][j] * y.

quiz.q: With int width 4 and float width 8, what is the offset of c in int a; float b; int c[10];?
quiz.explain: a takes 0 to 3, b takes 4 to 11, so c starts at 12.

quiz.q: For int M[3][4] in row-major order with base 1000 and width 4, where is M[2][1]?
Which three-address code is correct for a = b + - c?
options: t1 = minus c; t2 = b + t1; a = t2
t1 = b + c; a = minus t1
quiz.explain: The unary minus is computed first into t1, then added to b.

quiz.q: In column-major order, A[i1][i2] for an array with n1 rows is at:
quiz.explain: Columns are stored one after another, so i2 selects the column and i1 the position inside it.

quiz.q: How do compilers handle a variable declared in an inner block that hides an outer one?
options: One symbol table per scope, searched from inner to outer
They rename the outer variable at run time
quiz.explain: Chained symbol tables let the lookup find the innermost declaration first.

lessons.title: Control Flow, Boolean Expressions and Backpatching
lessons.content:
Imagine giving directions to a rickshaw puller in Old Dhaka before you know the full route. You say: at the next junction, if the road is blocked, turn left, and I will tell you later where to go after that. You write down a note: left-turn destination still unknown. A few minutes later, when you learn the destination, you fill in the note. Compilers face the same problem with jumps: when they emit a jump for an if or a while, they often do not yet know the address of the target. Backpatching is the technique of leaving blanks in jump instructions and filling them in later.

Why control flow is special: Expressions compute values, but statements like if, while and for decide which code runs next. In three-address code, the only tools for this are labels, unconditional jumps goto L, and conditional jumps like if x < y goto L. So the compiler must translate structured statements and boolean conditions into patterns of jumps. Doing this well matters, because conditions appear in almost every loop and branch.

Two ways to translate boolean expressions: One way treats a boolean like a number: compute 1 for true and 0 for false into a temporary, then test it. This is natural for b = x < y, where the value is stored. The other way, called jumping code or flow-of-control translation, never computes a value: the position reached in the code represents the result. For if ( x < y ) S, we just emit if x < y goto the code for S, otherwise jump past it. Jumping code is shorter and faster for conditions in if and while.

Numerical booleans when needed: Sometimes a boolean value really must be stored, as in flag = x < y && y < z. The compiler can still use jumping code and then turn the outcome into a number: at the true target it emits t = true and a jump past the next line, and at the false target it emits t = false, then assigns flag = t. So jumping code and numeric booleans are not enemies; the compiler picks whichever fits the context, and often combines them.

Short-circuit evaluation: In C, Java and most modern languages, in B1 || B2, if B1 is true, B2 is not evaluated at all; in B1 && B2, if B1 is false, B2 is skipped. This is not just a speed trick; programs rely on it, as in if ( p != NULL && p->value > 0 ), where evaluating the second part with a null p would crash. Jumping code implements short-circuit evaluation naturally: when B1 settles the answer, the code jumps straight to the right place.

Labels for the translation: We give each boolean expression B two inherited labels, B.true and B.false, the places to jump when B is true or false. Each statement S gets an inherited label S.next, the place to go after S finishes. Rules: B -> E1 rel E2 emits if E1.addr rel E2.addr goto B.true followed by goto B.false. B -> B1 || B2: B1.true = B.true, B1.false = a new label placed before B2's code, and B2.true = B.true, B2.false = B.false. B -> B1 && B2: B1.true = a new label placed before B2, B1.false = B.false, and B2 inherits B's labels. B -> ! B1 simply swaps true and false.

Translating if, if-else and while: For S -> if ( B ) S1: B.true is a new label placed right before S1's code, and B.false = S1.next = S.next. For S -> if ( B ) S1 else S2: B.true labels S1's code, B.false labels S2's code, and after S1 the code emits goto S.next so it skips S2. For S -> while ( B ) S1: a new label begin is placed before B's code, B.true labels S1's code, B.false = S.next, and after S1 the code emits goto begin to loop.

A worked example with labels: Translate if ( x < 100 || x > 200 && x != y ) x = 0;. Since && binds tighter, the condition is x < 100 || ( x > 200 && x != y ). Optimised jumping code: if x < 100 goto L2; ifFalse x > 200 goto L1; ifFalse x != y goto L1; L2: x = 0; L1: the next statement. If x < 100, we jump straight to the assignment, skipping the rest, which is short-circuiting in action. If x > 200 is false, the whole && part is false, so we jump to L1.

The problem with labels: In the label method, B.true and B.false are inherited: they must be known before B's code is generated. For a top-down parser that is fine. But in a single bottom-up pass, when we generate the jump for x < 100, we do not yet know where the then-part begins, because the parser has not reached it. One option is a second pass that resolves symbolic labels. Backpatching avoids the second pass.

The idea of backpatching: Emit jump instructions with their targets left blank, and keep lists of these incomplete jumps. When the target becomes known, go back and fill in every jump on the list. Three helper functions make this easy: makelist(i) creates a new list containing only instruction i; merge(p1, p2) joins two lists; backpatch(p, i) fills target i into every instruction on list p. A variable nextinstr holds the number of the next instruction to be generated.

Boolean expressions with backpatching: Each B gets two synthesized lists: B.truelist, jumps to fill with the target for true, and B.falselist, jumps for false. A marker nonterminal M -> ε records M.instr = nextinstr, the start of the code that follows it. Rules: B -> E1 rel E2: B.truelist = makelist(nextinstr); B.falselist = makelist(nextinstr + 1); emit if E1.addr rel E2.addr goto blank; emit goto blank. B -> B1 || M B2: backpatch(B1.falselist, M.instr); B.truelist = merge(B1.truelist, B2.truelist); B.falselist = B2.falselist. B -> B1 && M B2: backpatch(B1.truelist, M.instr); B.truelist = B2.truelist; B.falselist = merge(B1.falselist, B2.falselist). B -> ! B1 swaps the two lists. These are all synthesized, so they work in one bottom-up pass.

Tracing backpatching, part 1: Take x < 100 || x > 200 && x != y, with instructions numbered from 100. Reducing x < 100 emits 100: if x < 100 goto blank and 101: goto blank, with truelist {100} and falselist {101}. The marker before the right side records 102. Then x > 200 emits 102: if x > 200 goto blank and 103: goto blank, lists {102} and {103}. The marker before x != y records 104. Then x != y emits 104: if x != y goto blank and 105: goto blank, lists {104} and {105}.

Tracing backpatching, part 2: Now reduce the && part: backpatch the truelist {102} with 104, so 102 becomes if x > 200 goto 104. Its truelist is {104} and its falselist is {103, 105}. Then reduce the || part: backpatch the falselist {101} with 102, so 101 becomes goto 102. The whole expression has truelist {100, 104} and falselist {103, 105}. Those four jumps stay blank until the enclosing if statement knows where the then-part and the next statement begin.

Statements with backpatching: Statements get S.nextlist, the jumps that must go to the code after S. For S -> if ( B ) M S1: backpatch(B.truelist, M.instr); S.nextlist = merge(B.falselist, S1.nextlist). For S -> while M1 ( B ) M2 S1: backpatch(S1.nextlist, M1.instr), so the end of the body loops back to the test; backpatch(B.truelist, M2.instr); S.nextlist = B.falselist; and emit goto M1.instr. For if-else, an extra marker N emits a goto blank after S1 so the then-part skips the else-part, and that jump joins the nextlist. A sequence of statements backpatches each statement's nextlist to the start of the next statement.

Switch statements: A switch on an expression with many cases can be translated in different ways. If there are only a few cases, a chain of conditional jumps is fine: if t = 1 goto L1; if t = 2 goto L2; and so on. If the case values are many and close together, such as 0 to 20, a jump table is faster: the value is used as an index into an array of addresses, and one indirect jump goes straight to the right case. If values are many but spread out, a hash table or binary search can be used. Compilers choose based on how many cases there are and how dense they are.

Procedure calls: A call translates into evaluating each argument, emitting param for each, then a call instruction. For n = f ( a[i] ) with 4-byte elements: t1 = i * 4; t2 = a [ t1 ]; param t2; t3 = call f, 1; n = t3. The number 1 is the argument count. Inside f, code for return emits return with the value. The type checker has already verified the argument types against f's declaration.

Real life example 1, an online admission form: A university's admission site in Bangladesh checks: if SSC GPA is at least 4 and HSC GPA is at least 4, or the applicant has a special quota, allow the application. Thanks to short-circuit evaluation, if the quota check is placed first and is true, the GPA checks are skipped entirely. A programmer who knows this puts the cheapest and most decisive test first.
