Real life example 2, mobile banking menus: In a mobile banking app, a switch on the selected menu option, 1 for send money, 2 for cash out, up to 9, is usually compiled into a jump table, because the option values are small and dense. Tapping an option costs one table lookup and one jump, no matter how many options exist.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that && binds tighter than ||. Evaluating both sides of || when the first is true, which breaks short-circuit semantics. In backpatching, backpatching the wrong list: for || it is B1's falselist that goes to B2, and for && it is B1's truelist. Forgetting the goto after the then-part in if-else. Forgetting the jump back to the beginning in a while loop.

What exams ask: Translate if, if-else and while statements with compound conditions into three-address code using jumping code. Explain short-circuit evaluation. Give the backpatching rules for boolean expressions and statements and show the annotated parse tree or instruction sequence for an expression like x < 100 || x > 200 && x != y. Explain translation of switch statements and procedure calls.

Recap: Control flow is translated into labels and jumps. Boolean conditions are best translated as jumping code, which gives short-circuit evaluation for free. The label method uses inherited B.true, B.false and S.next. Backpatching does the same in one pass using lists of incomplete jumps, with makelist, merge and backpatch, and marker nonterminals that record instruction numbers. Switches use comparison chains or jump tables, and calls use param and call. Next lesson we look at what the running program needs at run time: stacks, activation records and parameter passing.
key_points: Control flow becomes labels, goto and conditional jumps; boolean conditions are best translated as jumping code.
Short-circuit: in B1 || B2, B2 is skipped if B1 is true; in B1 && B2, B2 is skipped if B1 is false.
Label method: B.true, B.false and S.next are inherited labels; while needs a begin label and a goto back.
Backpatching emits jumps with blank targets and fills them later using makelist, merge and backpatch.
B -> B1 || M B2: backpatch B1.falselist to M.instr; B -> B1 && M B2: backpatch B1.truelist to M.instr.
For x < 100 || x > 200 && x != y from 100: truelist {100, 104}, falselist {103, 105}.
Switch uses a comparison chain or a jump table for dense values; calls emit param for each argument, then call f, n.
lessons.tip: When tracing backpatching, keep a small table with three columns: instruction number, instruction, and target (blank or filled). Fill targets in pencil as each backpatch happens.
lessons.task: Write jumping code with labels for while ( a < b && c > d ) a = a + 1;. Then redo it with backpatching, numbering instructions from 200, and list truelist, falselist and nextlist at each step.

quiz.q: With short-circuit evaluation, when is B2 skipped in B1 && B2?
quiz.explain: If B1 is false, the whole && is false, so B2 is not evaluated.

quiz.q: In B -> B1 || M B2 with backpatching, which list is backpatched to M.instr?
quiz.explain: If B1 is false, control must go to B2, which starts at M.instr.

quiz.q: Why is backpatching useful?
options: It fills jump targets later, allowing one-pass generation
quiz.explain: Targets unknown when a jump is emitted are filled once they become known.

quiz.q: In the translation of while ( B ) S1, what does the code emit after S1?
options: goto begin, back to the test of B
quiz.explain: After the body, control returns to re-test the condition.

quiz.q: When is a jump table a good translation for a switch statement?
options: When case values are many and densely packed
When there are exactly two cases
quiz.explain: Dense values can index an array of addresses, giving one lookup and one jump.

lessons.title: Run-Time Environments: Stack, Heap and Activation Records
lessons.content:
Imagine a busy office at Motijheel where every officer who starts a new task takes a fresh sheet of paper from a pile, writes the task details on it, and puts it on top of the pile. If that task needs another officer's help, the helper puts his own sheet on top. When the helper finishes, he removes his sheet, and the first officer continues with his own sheet now on top again. The pile of sheets is the run-time stack, and each sheet is an activation record. This lesson explains what a running program needs in memory: where code and data live, how function calls are organised, how parameters are passed, and how dynamically created objects are managed.

What the run-time environment is: The compiler translates names in the source program, such as variables and functions, into addresses in the target machine. But many things are only known while the program runs: how many times a recursive function calls itself, how many objects a user creates, which function called which. The run-time environment is the set of memory layouts and conventions, agreed between the compiler, the operating system and the target machine, that make the generated code work. The compiler generates code that follows these conventions.

Storage organisation: A typical program's memory is divided into areas. The code area holds the machine instructions; its size is known at compile time. The static area holds global variables and constants whose size and lifetime are fixed. The rest is shared by two dynamic areas that grow towards each other: the stack, which holds activation records for function calls, and the heap, which holds data allocated explicitly at run time, such as objects created with new or malloc. Placing them at opposite ends lets either grow as needed until they meet.

Static vs dynamic allocation: Static allocation decides addresses at compile time. Early FORTRAN allocated everything statically, which is simple and fast but has two big limits: no recursion, because each function has only one fixed place for its locals, and no data structures whose size depends on input. Stack allocation solves recursion: each call gets fresh space. Heap allocation solves data that must outlive the function that created it, such as a linked list node returned to the caller.

Activations and the activation tree: Each execution of a function is called an activation. For a program where main calls fact(3), which calls fact(2), which calls fact(1), the activations form a tree: main is the root, fact(3) its child, fact(2) its grandchild and fact(1) at the bottom. If main also called print after fact returned, print would be another child of main, to the right of fact(3). The sequence of calls corresponds to a preorder walk of this tree, and the returns to a postorder walk. At any moment, the live activations are exactly those on the path from the root to the current node.

The control stack: Because live activations always form a path, a stack is the perfect structure for them. When a function is called, a new activation record is pushed; when it returns, the record is popped. While fact(1) is running, the stack holds records for main, fact(3), fact(2) and fact(1), in that order from bottom to top. This is the same stack you saw in assembly with CALL, RET, PUSH and POP; now we understand how a compiler organises it.

The activation record: An activation record, also called a frame, holds the information needed for one activation. A typical record has these fields: the actual parameters passed by the caller; space for the returned value; the control link, which points to the caller's activation record, also called the dynamic link; the access link, which points to the record of the enclosing function in nested languages, also called the static link; the saved machine status, such as the return address and saved registers; local data for the function's variables; and temporaries for intermediate values. Real compilers often pass the first few parameters and the return value in registers instead of memory.

Calling and return sequences: The calling sequence is the code that sets up an activation record; the return sequence restores the state afterwards. The work is divided between caller and callee. Typically, the caller evaluates the actual parameters, stores the return address and the old stack pointer into the new record, and jumps to the callee. The callee saves the registers it will use and initialises its locals. On return, the callee places the return value where the caller expects it, restores the saved registers and the stack pointer, and jumps to the return address. Putting as much work as possible in the callee keeps code size smaller, because a function is defined once but called from many places.

Variable-length data: Some languages allow local arrays whose size depends on a parameter. Their size is not known at compile time, so the activation record holds a pointer to the array, and the array itself is placed on the stack just after the fixed-size part of the record. The compiler can still access the fixed fields at known offsets from the frame pointer, and reaches the array through the pointer.

Non-local data without nesting: In C, a function can access its own locals and global variables, but functions cannot be nested inside other functions. Globals are in the static area at fixed addresses, and locals are at fixed offsets in the current activation record. So no special links are needed to find any variable. This simplicity is one reason C compilers are fast and C function calls are cheap.

Nested procedures and access links: Languages like Pascal, Ada, ML and also nested functions in Python and JavaScript allow a function to be defined inside another and use the outer function's variables. Suppose q is nested inside p, and q uses p's variable x. When q runs, it must find the most recent activation of p, which may not be its caller, for instance if q calls itself recursively. The access link in q's record points to the record of the lexically enclosing function, p. If q is at nesting depth nq and x belongs to a function at depth np, q follows nq minus np access links to reach the right record, then uses x's known offset.

Displays: Following a chain of access links can be slow for deeply nested programs. A display is an array d, where d[i] points to the most recent activation record of a function at nesting depth i. To reach a variable at depth i, the code just loads d[i] and adds the offset, one memory access no matter how deep the nesting. Each activation must save and restore the display entry for its depth, which is cheap.

Parameter passing, value and reference: In call by value, the caller evaluates the argument and copies the value into the callee's parameter; changes inside the callee do not affect the caller. C and Java use call by value; Java object references are themselves passed by value. In call by reference, the caller passes the address of the argument; the parameter is an alias, so changes are visible to the caller. C++ reference parameters and Pascal var parameters work this way. For void swap(int x, int y) in C, swapping inside the function does not change the caller's variables; with references it does.

Value-result and name: Call by value-result, also called copy-restore, copies the value in at the call, works on the local copy, and copies the final value back to the argument at return. Call by name, from Algol 60, behaves as if the argument expression were substituted textually for the parameter, re-evaluated every time it is used; it is implemented with small hidden functions called thunks and is mostly of historical interest, though it inspired lazy evaluation.

A classic comparison: Let p(x, y) execute x = x + 1; y = y + 1, and call p(a, a) with a = 1. By value: x and y are copies, so a stays 1. By reference: x and y are both aliases of a, so a is incremented twice and becomes 3. By value-result: x and y each start as 1 and each become 2, then both are copied back to a, so a ends as 2. Three methods, three different answers, which is why exams love this example.

Heap management: The heap is managed by a memory manager that handles allocation and deallocation. Allocation finds a free block large enough, using strategies such as first fit, taking the first block that fits, or best fit, taking the smallest block that fits. Over time, the heap can become fragmented into many small free holes that cannot satisfy a large request. Coalescing merges neighbouring free blocks into bigger ones. In C, the programmer calls malloc and free explicitly; mistakes cause memory leaks, when memory is never freed, or dangling pointers, when freed memory is still used.

Garbage collection: Languages like Java, C#, Python and Go free memory automatically. An object is garbage when no chain of references from the program's roots, such as globals and stack variables, reaches it. Reference counting keeps a count of references to each object and frees it when the count drops to zero; it is simple and immediate, but cannot free cycles of objects that refer to each other. Mark-and-sweep marks every object reachable from the roots, then sweeps the heap and frees the unmarked ones. Copying collectors move live objects to a fresh area, compacting them. Generational collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young, collecting the young area often and the old area rarely.

Real life example 1, stack overflow in a student program: A student in Khulna writes a recursive function to compute factorial but forgets the base case. Each call pushes a new activation record, the stack keeps growing, and the program crashes with a stack overflow error. Understanding activation records makes this error obvious: infinite recursion means infinite records, and the stack has a fixed size.

Real life example 2, a memory leak in a server: A ride-sharing backend written in C++ allocates a new object for every ride request but sometimes forgets to free it. Over a busy Eid holiday the process slowly uses more and more memory until it is restarted. The same service written in Java or Go would have its unused objects collected automatically, at the cost of occasional garbage collection work.

Common mistakes: Confusing the control link, which points to the caller, with the access link, which points to the lexically enclosing function. Thinking Java passes objects by reference; it passes references by value. Forgetting that static allocation forbids recursion. Mixing up first fit and best fit. Thinking reference counting can free cyclic structures. Getting the p(a, a) example wrong by not tracking aliasing carefully.

What exams ask: Draw the storage organisation of a program. Draw the activation tree and the control stack at a given moment for a recursive program. Describe the fields of an activation record. Explain calling and return sequences. Explain access links and displays for nested procedures. Compare call by value, reference, value-result and name with an example. Short notes on heap management, fragmentation and garbage collection.

Recap: The run-time environment lays memory out as code, static data, stack and heap. Each function call creates an activation record on the stack, with parameters, return value, control and access links, saved status, locals and temporaries; calling and return sequences build and remove it. Nested languages reach outer variables with access links or displays. Parameters may be passed by value, reference, value-result or name, with different results under aliasing. The heap is managed manually or by garbage collection. Next lesson we start generating real target code.
key_points: Memory is organised into code, static data, stack and heap; stack and heap grow towards each other.
Each function execution is an activation; live activations lie on one path of the activation tree, so a stack holds them.
An activation record holds parameters, return value, control link, access link, saved machine status, locals and temporaries.
Calling and return sequences split work between caller and callee to set up and tear down the record.
Access links (static links) and displays let nested functions reach variables of lexically enclosing functions.
For p(x, y) { x = x + 1; y = y + 1 } called as p(a, a) with a = 1: value gives 1, reference gives 3, value-result gives 2.
Heap: first fit / best fit, fragmentation and coalescing; garbage collection by reference counting, mark-and-sweep, copying or generational methods.
lessons.tip: For parameter-passing questions, draw boxes for each variable and arrows for aliases, then execute the statements one by one. Aliasing errors disappear when you can see the arrows.
lessons.task: Write a recursive function that computes the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n. Draw the activation tree for n = 3 and the control stack at the moment the deepest call is running, labelling each record's fields.

quiz.q: Which field of an activation record points to the caller's activation record?
quiz.explain: The control (dynamic) link points to the caller; the access link points to the lexically enclosing function.

quiz.q: Why could early FORTRAN, with only static allocation, not support recursion?
options: It had no stack pointer register
Each function had only one fixed place for its locals
quiz.explain: A recursive call would overwrite the locals of the activation still in progress.

quiz.q: p(x, y) does x = x + 1; y = y + 1. With a = 1, after p(a, a) by reference, a is:
quiz.explain: Both x and y alias a, so a is incremented twice.

quiz.q: What is a display used for?
options: Fast access to activation records of enclosing functions at each nesting depth
quiz.explain: d[i] points to the most recent record at depth i, avoiding long access-link chains.

quiz.q: Which garbage collection method cannot free cycles of objects on its own?
quiz.explain: Objects in a cycle keep each other's counts above zero even when unreachable.

lessons.title: Code Generation: Target Machine, Basic Blocks and Flow Graphs
lessons.content:
Imagine a delivery company in Dhaka that receives a list of orders written in plain language: deliver 3 boxes to Banani, collect payment, return to the warehouse. A dispatcher must turn that list into exact instructions for real riders and real motorbikes: which rider, which bike, which roads, in which order, while using as little fuel and time as possible. The bikes have limited storage, like a processor has a limited number of registers. The code generator is that dispatcher. It turns intermediate code into real machine instructions, choosing instructions, registers and order so that the program runs correctly and fast.

What the code generator does: The code generator is the last phase of the compiler. Its input is intermediate code, such as three-address code, plus the symbol table, which tells it where every name lives. Its output is the target program: machine code, relocatable object code, or assembly language. The most important requirement is still correctness: the generated code must do exactly what the intermediate code says. After that, it should make good use of the machine, especially its registers.

The main issues: Code generation involves three intertwined problems. Instruction selection: which target instructions implement each IR operation, since one operation may have many possible translations with different costs. Register allocation and assignment: which values should live in registers at each point, and in which specific register, since registers are far faster than memory but very few. Evaluation order: in what order to compute values, since some orders need fewer registers. Finding the best solution for these together is NP-complete in general, so compilers use good heuristics.

A simple target machine: To reason about code, textbooks use a simple register machine. It has registers R0, R1 and so on, and instructions such as LD r, x to load a value from memory location x into register r; ST x, r to store register r into x; arithmetic like ADD r1, r2, r3, which puts r2 + r3 into r1, and SUB, MUL similarly; an unconditional jump BR L; and conditional jumps like BLTZ r, L, which jumps to L if r is less than zero. This looks very much like real RISC processors such as ARM and RISC-V.

Addressing modes: The machine supports several ways to name an operand. A variable name x refers to its memory location. An indexed address a(r) means the location at address a plus the contents of register r, which is how array elements are reached. A constant is written with #, as in LD R1, #100, loading the number 100. Indirect addressing *r means the location whose address is held in r. The mode *100(r) means the location whose address is stored at 100 plus the contents of r.

Instruction cost: To compare different translations, we give each instruction a cost: 1 for the instruction itself plus 1 for each operand that is a memory address or a constant, because those need an extra word in the instruction. So LD R0, R1 costs 1, LD R0, M costs 2, and LD R1, *100(R2) costs 2. For x = y - z, the straightforward code LD R1, y; LD R2, z; SUB R1, R1, R2; ST x, R1 costs 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 7. The goal is to reduce this total.

Why naive translation is wasteful: Translating each three-address instruction separately produces correct but poor code. For a = b + c; d = a + e, a naive generator emits LD R0, b; LD R1, c; ADD R0, R0, R1; ST a, R0; LD R0, a; LD R1, e; ADD R0, R0, R1; ST d, R0. The fifth instruction, LD R0, a, is useless, because R0 already holds a. And if a is not used afterwards, even the store into a is unnecessary. Good code generation keeps track of what is in each register to avoid such waste.

Basic blocks: To work well, the code generator splits the intermediate code into basic blocks. A basic block is a maximal sequence of consecutive instructions with two properties: control can only enter at the first instruction, and control leaves only at the last instruction, with no jumps into or out of the middle. Inside a block, instructions always run one after another, all of them, which makes analysis simple and safe.

Finding leaders: Blocks are found with a simple rule for leaders, the first instructions of blocks. Rule 1: the first instruction of the program is a leader. Rule 2: any instruction that is the target of a jump, conditional or unconditional, is a leader. Rule 3: any instruction that immediately follows a jump is a leader. Each basic block consists of a leader and all instructions up to, but not including, the next leader.

A worked example: Consider code that sums an array and computes the average: 1: s = 0; 2: i = 0; 3: if i >= n goto 9; 4: t1 = i * 4; 5: t2 = a [ t1 ]; 6: s = s + t2; 7: i = i + 1; 8: goto 3; 9: avg = s / n. Leaders: instruction 1, by rule 1. Instruction 3, because it is the target of the jump at 8. Instruction 9, because it is the target of the jump at 3. Instruction 4, because it follows the jump at 3. Instruction 9 also follows the jump at 8. So the leaders are 1, 3, 4 and 9, giving blocks B1 = 1 to 2, B2 = 3, B3 = 4 to 8, and B4 = 9.

Flow graphs: A flow graph shows the blocks as nodes and possible transfers of control as edges. There is an edge from block B to block C if C can run immediately after B: either the last instruction of B jumps to the leader of C, or C immediately follows B and B does not end in an unconditional jump. In our example the edges are B1 to B2, B2 to B3 because the conditional jump can fall through, B2 to B4 when the jump is taken, and B3 to B2 because of goto 3. We also add an entry node pointing to B1 and an exit node after B4.

Loops in the flow graph: B2 and B3 form a loop: control can go around B2, B3, B2, B3 many times. Loops matter enormously, because programs spend most of their time inside them. Optimizations in lessons 24 and 25, such as moving loop-invariant work out of the loop, need to find loops in the flow graph first. Formally, a loop has a single entry block, called the header, here B2, that dominates all blocks in the loop.

Next-use and liveness: Within a block, the code generator wants to know, for each name, whether its current value will be used again, and where. A name is live at a point if its value will be used later; its next use is the next instruction that reads it. These are computed by scanning the block backwards from the last instruction. For each instruction x = y op z, first attach to the instruction the current information about x, y and z; then mark x as not live with no next use, because this instruction overwrites it; then mark y and z as live with next use at this instruction. At the end of the block, temporaries are usually dead and user variables are assumed live.

Register and address descriptors: A simple code generator keeps two tables. The register descriptor records, for each register, which variables' current values it holds. The address descriptor records, for each variable, all the places where its current value can be found: a register, its memory location, or both. With these, the generator knows when a value is already in a register, so no load is needed, and which values must be stored before a register is reused or at the end of the block.

The getReg function: For each instruction x = y + z, the generator calls getReg to choose registers Ry and Rz for the operands and Rx for the result. If y is already in a register, use it; otherwise pick a free register, or one whose value is also safely in memory, or, as a last resort, spill a value by storing it. Then emit LD Ry, y only if y is not already in Ry, the same for z, and finally ADD Rx, Ry, Rz. Update the descriptors: Rx now holds only x, and x's only current location is Rx until it is stored.

A small trace: For the block t = a - b; u = a - c; v = t + u; a = d; d = v + u, with t, u and v temporaries and three registers, a good generator produces: LD R1, a; LD R2, b; SUB R2, R1, R2, so R2 holds t. LD R3, c; SUB R1, R1, R3, so R1 holds u. ADD R3, R2, R1, so R3 holds v. LD R2, d, and since a = d is a copy, R2 now holds both a and d. ADD R1, R3, R1, so R1 holds the new d. At the end of the block, the live variables a and d are stored: ST a, R2; ST d, R1. No value is loaded twice.

Real life example 1, Android phones: When an app is installed on an Android phone, the Android runtime compiles app bytecode into native ARM code using a code generator like the one in this lesson. On a cheap phone with a slow memory system, keeping values in registers instead of reloading them makes a visible difference in speed and battery life.

Real life example 2, a bus route plan: A transport planner in Chattogram divides each bus route into segments between stops where buses can turn or branch. Within a segment, the bus simply goes stop after stop with no choices, like a basic block. The route map showing segments and possible turns is a flow graph, and the circular route that buses repeat all day is a loop where improvements save the most time.

Common mistakes: Forgetting rule 3 for leaders, the instruction after a jump. Making a block that contains a jump target in its middle. Missing the fall-through edge from a conditional jump. Counting instruction cost without the extra 1 for memory or constant operands. Forgetting to store live variables at the end of a block. Computing next-use information forwards instead of backwards.

What exams ask: Explain the issues in the design of a code generator. Describe a simple target machine and compute the cost of given instruction sequences. Partition given three-address code into basic blocks using the leader rules and draw the flow graph. Explain next-use information. Explain register and address descriptors and generate code for a basic block using getReg.

Recap: The code generator maps IR to target code, facing instruction selection, register allocation and evaluation order. A simple RISC-like machine with LD, ST, arithmetic and branches, plus cost per instruction, lets us compare translations. Basic blocks are found with three leader rules and connected into a flow graph, where loops become visible. Next-use information and register and address descriptors let a simple generator avoid useless loads and stores. Next lesson we allocate registers across whole regions and clean up code with peephole optimization.
key_points: The code generator turns IR into target code; its problems are instruction selection, register allocation and evaluation order.
Simple target machine: LD, ST, ADD/SUB/MUL r1, r2, r3, BR, conditional branches; addressing modes x, a(r), #c, *r.
Instruction cost = 1 + 1 for each memory or constant operand; x = y - z with two loads, SUB and ST costs 7.
Leaders: the first instruction, any jump target, and any instruction right after a jump; a basic block runs from a leader to before the next leader.
A flow graph has blocks as nodes and edges for jumps and fall-through; loops in it are where optimization pays most.
Next-use and liveness are computed by scanning a block backwards.
Register and address descriptors plus getReg avoid redundant loads; live variables are stored at the end of the block.
lessons.tip: When finding basic blocks, first circle every jump and its target in the code, then mark leaders with the three rules. Blocks then fall out naturally.
lessons.task: Write three-address code for: f = 1; i = 1; while (i <= n) { f = f * i; i = i + 1; } Then find the leaders, the basic blocks and draw the flow graph, marking the loop.

quiz.q: Which instruction is NOT a leader by the standard rules?
options: The first instruction of the program
The target of a conditional jump
An instruction immediately after a jump
An instruction immediately after a copy statement
quiz.explain: Only the first instruction, jump targets and instructions after jumps are leaders.

quiz.q: Using cost = 1 + 1 per memory or constant operand, what does LD R0, M cost?
quiz.explain: 1 for the instruction plus 1 because M is a memory address.

quiz.q: When is there an edge from block B to block C in a flow graph?
options: When C is longer than B
When B and C use the same variables
When C can execute immediately after B
Always, between every pair of blocks
quiz.explain: Edges show possible transfers of control: jumps or fall-through.

quiz.q: In which direction is next-use information computed within a block?
options: Forwards, from first to last instruction
Backwards, from last to first instruction
Only at the end of the program
quiz.explain: Scanning backwards lets each use be known before reaching the definition that precedes it.

quiz.q: What does the address descriptor record?
options: Where the current value of each variable can be found
quiz.explain: It lists, for each variable, the registers and/or memory location holding its current value.

lessons.title: Register Allocation and Peephole Optimization
lessons.content:
Think of a small tea stall in Sylhet with only three cups on the counter but many customers. The owner must decide who gets a cup now, and who has to wait. Two customers who are drinking at the same time cannot share a cup, but a customer who left at 4 pm and one who arrived at 4:30 can use the same cup, after a wash. Registers are the processor's few cups. Register allocation decides which values sit in which register and when, so that values in use at the same time never share a register, and as few values as possible are pushed out to slow memory.

Why registers matter: Registers are the fastest storage in a computer, inside the processor itself. A memory access, even when the cache helps, is slower, and a miss in the cache can cost hundreds of cycles. But registers are few: x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers and 64-bit ARM has 31. A program may have hundreds of variables and temporaries. Deciding which of them deserve registers is one of the most important jobs of an optimizing compiler, often making a bigger difference than any other single optimization.

Allocation vs assignment: Register allocation decides which values will be kept in registers at each point of the program. Register assignment decides exactly which register each value gets. The simple generator in lesson 22 did both locally, inside one basic block, and stored everything at the end of the block. Global register allocation works across blocks and loops, which matters because a variable used in every iteration of a loop should stay in a register for the whole loop, not be stored and reloaded at each block boundary.

A usage-count heuristic: A simple global approach is to give registers to the variables used most often inside loops. For each variable, estimate the savings from keeping it in a register: roughly one unit for each use inside the loop that would otherwise need a load, plus extra savings if the variable would otherwise have to be stored at the end of a block where it is live. Variables with the largest savings get the registers. This is easy, but graph colouring, which considers exactly which values are alive together, gives better results.

Liveness and live ranges: A variable is live at a point if its current value may be used later. Its live range is the set of points where it is live, from its definition to its last use. Two variables whose live ranges overlap must be in different registers, because both values are needed at the same time. Two variables whose live ranges do not overlap can share a register. Liveness across a whole function is computed by data-flow analysis, which lesson 25 explains; inside a straight piece of code we can just read it off.

The interference graph: Build a graph with one node for each variable or temporary. Draw an edge between two nodes if they are live at the same time somewhere in the program; we say they interfere. Assigning registers then becomes colouring the graph: give each node a colour, one colour per register, so that no edge connects two nodes of the same colour. If the graph can be coloured with k colours and the machine has k registers, every variable gets a register and none needs memory.

A worked example: Consider 1: a = 1; 2: b = 2; 3: c = a + b; 4: d = c * 2; 5: e = d + b; 6: return e. Live sets after each instruction: after 1, {a}; after 2, {a, b}; after 3, {b, c}, since a is dead after its last use; after 4, {b, d}; after 5, {e}. So the edges are a with b, b with c and b with d. The graph is a star with b in the middle. Two colours are enough: b gets R1, and a, c, d all get R2, because they never interfere with each other; e interferes with nothing and can take either. Five variables fit in two registers.

Colouring with Chaitin's idea: Finding the minimum number of colours is NP-complete in general, so compilers use a heuristic introduced by Gregory Chaitin and colleagues at IBM around 1981. The key observation: if a node has fewer than k neighbours, then whatever colours they get, at least one colour is left for it. So remove such a node from the graph and push it on a stack; removing it lowers its neighbours' degrees, so more nodes become removable. Repeat. If the graph becomes empty, pop the nodes one by one and give each a colour not used by its already-coloured neighbours. This always succeeds.

Spilling: If at some point every remaining node has k or more neighbours, the heuristic is stuck. Then one node is chosen to spill: its value will live in memory instead of a register. The compiler inserts a store after each definition and a load before each use, which splits its long live range into tiny ones. The node is removed, and colouring continues. A good choice for spilling is a variable with few uses, especially uses outside loops, and with many neighbours, so its removal helps the most. Spilling costs time, so allocators try hard to minimise it.

Coalescing copies: Copy instructions like x = y are common after other optimizations. If x and y do not interfere, they can be given the same register, and then the copy becomes x = x and can be deleted. In the interference graph this means merging the two nodes, called coalescing. Coalescing must be careful not to create a node with too many neighbours, or it may cause new spills; modern allocators use conservative rules for when to coalesce.

Instruction selection by tree patterns: Choosing instructions can also be done systematically. The IR for a statement is viewed as a tree, and each machine instruction is described as a small tree pattern with a cost. For example, an indexed load pattern matches a memory read of base plus register in one instruction. The code generator covers the IR tree with patterns, a process called tiling. A greedy method called maximal munch takes the biggest pattern that fits at each node; dynamic programming can find the cheapest cover. Tools called code-generator generators build such selectors from a machine description.

Peephole optimization: After code generation, the code can be polished by peephole optimization. The idea is to slide a small window, the peephole, over the instructions, a few at a time, and replace any sequence inside it with a shorter or faster equivalent. Each improvement may create new opportunities, so the process is repeated until nothing changes. It is simple, fast, and surprisingly effective, and it works on target code or on intermediate code.

Redundant loads and stores: Consider ST a, R0 followed directly by LD R0, a. The load is useless, because R0 already holds the value of a. The peephole optimizer deletes the load, as long as it is not the target of a jump, which would mean control could arrive there with a different R0. This one pattern cleans up much of the waste left by simple code generators.

Unreachable code and jumps to jumps: An unlabelled instruction right after an unconditional jump can never run, so it can be removed. Code guarded by a condition that is constant can also disappear: if a constant debug flag is 0, the code if debug == 1 goto L1; goto L2; L1: print information; L2: can first become if debug != 1 goto L2; print information; L2:, and since debug != 1 is always true, the print becomes unreachable and is deleted. Jumps to jumps are shortened too: goto L1 where L1: goto L2 becomes goto L2, and if nothing else jumps to L1, that instruction can go.

Algebraic simplification and strength reduction: Instructions like x = x + 0 or x = x * 1 do nothing and can be deleted. Strength reduction replaces an expensive operation with a cheaper one: x squared can become x * x instead of a call to a power function; multiplication by 2 can become an addition x + x or a left shift; division of an unsigned value by a power of 2 can become a right shift. These must be applied carefully: shifting a negative signed number right does not always equal integer division in C, so compilers add a small correction for signed values.

Machine idioms: Many processors have special instructions that do common jobs cheaply. Some can increment a register in one short instruction, so i = i + 1 can use it. Some have auto-increment addressing, which reads a value and moves a pointer to the next element in one step, perfect for walking through arrays. Some have fused multiply-add. The peephole optimizer, or the instruction selector, recognises patterns that match these idioms and uses them.

Real life example 1, mobile games: A game on a phone updates the positions of hundreds of objects every frame, 60 times a second. The inner loop that updates positions uses a handful of variables: x, y, speed, and a loop counter. A good register allocator keeps all of them in registers for the whole loop. If it spilled them, each frame would need thousands of extra memory accesses, and the game would stutter on a budget phone.

Real life example 2, a university exam routine: An exam controller in Dhaka must assign exam slots to courses so that no two courses taken by the same student are at the same time. Courses are nodes, an edge joins courses that share a student, and time slots are colours. It is the same graph colouring problem as register allocation, and the same heuristics work: schedule courses with fewer conflicts first, and if slots run out, move one course to an extra day, which is like spilling.

Common mistakes: Adding an interference edge between variables that are never live at the same time. Forgetting that a variable stops being live after its last use, not at the end of the block. Thinking graph colouring always finds the minimum number of colours quickly; the heuristic is fast but not always optimal. Deleting a load that is a jump target. Applying shift-for-division to signed negative numbers without correction.

What exams ask: Explain register allocation and assignment and why global allocation matters. Build the interference graph for a given code fragment and colour it with k registers, showing spills if necessary. Explain Chaitin's simplify and select approach. List peephole optimizations with examples: redundant loads and stores, unreachable code, flow-of-control optimization, algebraic simplification, strength reduction and use of machine idioms.

Recap: Registers are fast but few, so the compiler must decide which values live in them. Liveness gives live ranges; overlapping ranges become edges of the interference graph, and k-colouring the graph assigns k registers. Chaitin's heuristic removes nodes with fewer than k neighbours, spills when stuck, and colours on the way back; coalescing removes copies. Peephole optimization then polishes the code through a small window: removing redundant loads, unreachable code and jumps to jumps, simplifying algebra, reducing strength and using machine idioms. Next lesson we look at bigger, machine-independent optimizations.
key_points: Registers are much faster than memory but few (16 general-purpose on x86-64, 31 on 64-bit ARM).
Two variables interfere if they are live at the same time; the interference graph has an edge for each such pair.
Assigning k registers = colouring the interference graph with k colours.
Chaitin's heuristic: repeatedly remove nodes with fewer than k neighbours onto a stack, then pop and colour; if stuck, spill a node.
Spilling keeps a variable in memory with a store after each definition and a load before each use.
Coalescing merges non-interfering nodes connected by a copy so the copy can be deleted.
Peephole optimizations: redundant load/store removal, unreachable code, jumps to jumps, algebraic simplification, strength reduction, machine idioms.
lessons.tip: To build an interference graph, write the live set after every instruction in a column first. Then every pair inside the same live set is an edge; you will not miss any.
lessons.task: For the code x = 5; y = x + 1; z = y * 2; w = x + z; v = w - y; return v, compute live sets, draw the interference graph and colour it with as few registers as possible. Then apply peephole rules to: ST a, R1; LD R1, a; ADD R1, R1, #0; goto L1; L1: goto L2.

quiz.q: When do two variables interfere?
options: When they have the same name
When they are live at the same point in the program
When they are in the same basic block
quiz.explain: Values needed at the same time cannot share a register.

quiz.q: In Chaitin's approach, which nodes can safely be removed first?
options: Nodes with more than k neighbours
Nodes with fewer than k neighbours
quiz.explain: A node with fewer than k neighbours is guaranteed a free colour later.

quiz.q: What does spilling a variable mean?
options: Keeping it in memory, with stores after definitions and loads before uses
Moving it into the code area
quiz.explain: Spilled values live in memory, split into short live ranges around each use.

quiz.q: Which peephole change is safe only if the instruction is not a jump target?
options: Shortening goto L1 when L1: goto L2
Deleting LD R0, a right after ST a, R0
quiz.explain: If control could jump to the load, R0 might hold a different value there.

quiz.explain: An expensive operation is replaced with a cheaper equivalent.

lessons.title: Machine-Independent Optimization
lessons.content:
Imagine a clerk at a land office in Rajshahi who must prepare a report on 500 plots. For every plot, he walks to the cabinet to fetch the same district map, uses it for a minute, and puts it back. A smarter clerk fetches the map once, keeps it on his desk, and saves hundreds of trips. He also notices that he copies the same total into three different forms; he computes it once and reuses it. Nothing about the report changes, but the work takes a fraction of the time. Compiler optimization does exactly this to programs: it removes repeated work, needless copies and wasted steps, without changing what the program does.

What optimization means: An optimization is a transformation of the program that makes it better, usually faster, sometimes smaller or more energy efficient, while preserving its meaning. The word is a bit of an exaggeration: compilers rarely produce truly optimal code, they just improve it. Every transformation must be safe: for every possible input, the optimized program must produce the same observable results as the original. A transformation that is fast but sometimes wrong is not an optimization; it is a bug.

Machine-independent vs machine-dependent: Machine-independent optimizations work on intermediate code and do not depend on the target processor: removing common subexpressions or moving work out of loops helps on any machine. Machine-dependent optimizations, like register allocation, instruction selection and peephole rules using special instructions, were the subject of the previous lesson. In a modern compiler such as GCC or LLVM, the middle end runs dozens of machine-independent passes over the IR before the back end generates code.

Local vs global: Local optimizations work within a single basic block, where control flows straight through, so reasoning is easy. Global optimizations, also called intraprocedural, work across the whole flow graph of a function, which needs data-flow analysis to know what is true at each point, the subject of the next lesson. Interprocedural optimizations work across function boundaries, for example inlining a small function at its call site, which removes call overhead and opens up more optimization.

Common subexpression elimination: An expression E is a common subexpression if it was computed before and none of its operands have changed since. Then the earlier result can be reused. In t1 = 4 * i; t2 = a [ t1 ]; t3 = 4 * i; t4 = b [ t3 ], the second 4 * i is common, so it becomes t1 = 4 * i; t2 = a [ t1 ]; t4 = b [ t1 ]. Array indexing creates many such expressions, because the source code a[i] + b[i] hides two identical address calculations. Global CSE does the same across blocks, when the expression is available on every path.

Copy propagation: After a copy x = y, later uses of x can use y instead, as long as neither x nor y has been changed in between. For example, x = t1; a = x + 1 becomes x = t1; a = t1 + 1. On its own this saves nothing, but it often makes the copy itself dead, so dead code elimination can then delete it. CSE frequently creates copies, so copy propagation and dead code elimination usually follow it.

Constant folding and constant propagation: Constant folding evaluates expressions whose operands are all constants at compile time: x = 2 * 3.14 becomes x = 6.28. Constant propagation replaces a variable known to hold a constant with that constant: after n = 10, a later y = n * 4 becomes y = 10 * 4, which folding turns into y = 40. Together they can make conditions constant, such as if n > 5, which then lets the compiler delete the branch that can never run.

Dead code elimination: A statement is dead if it computes a value that is never used. If x = y + 1 is followed by code that never reads x before overwriting it or before the function ends, the statement can be removed, provided it has no side effects like I/O or a function call that might change something. Unreachable code, which control can never reach, can also be deleted. Dead code arises often from other optimizations and from code that is guarded by a constant debug flag.

Loops matter most: Programs spend most of their time in loops, especially inner loops, so loop optimizations give the biggest gains. Saving one instruction inside a loop that runs a million times saves a million instructions; saving one outside the loop saves one. The three classic loop optimizations are code motion, induction variable elimination, and strength reduction.

Code motion: An expression is loop-invariant if its value does not change from one iteration to the next, because its operands are constants or are defined only outside the loop. Code motion moves such computations to just before the loop, into a block called the preheader. For example, while ( i <= limit - 2 ) recomputes limit - 2 on every test, assuming limit does not change in the loop. After code motion: t = limit - 2; while ( i <= t ). The computation now happens once instead of on every iteration.

Induction variables: A variable is an induction variable if it changes by a fixed amount in each iteration, like i = i + 1, or if it is a linear function of another induction variable, like t1 = 4 * i. When two induction variables move in lock-step, one of them may be eliminated. If i is used only to compute t1 and in the loop test i <= 10, the test can be rewritten as t1 <= 40, and i disappears from the loop.

Strength reduction in loops: Multiplication is more expensive than addition on many machines. If t1 = 4 * i is computed in every iteration and i increases by 1 each time, then t1 increases by 4 each time. So instead of multiplying, initialise t1 = 4 * i once before the loop and add t1 = t1 + 4 each time i is incremented. This replaces a multiplication with an addition in the loop, and it is exactly what makes walking through an array cheap.

A worked loop example: Consider the code for summing an array: i = 0; L: t1 = 4 * i; t2 = a [ t1 ]; s = s + t2; i = i + 1; if i < n goto L. Strength reduction: t1 = 0 before the loop, and t1 = t1 + 4 instead of t1 = 4 * i. Induction variable elimination: if i is not used after the loop, replace the test i < n with t1 < t3, where t3 = 4 * n is computed once before the loop. Now the loop is: L: t2 = a [ t1 ]; s = s + t2; t1 = t1 + 4; if t1 < t3 goto L. Four instructions per iteration, no multiplication.

DAGs for local optimization: Inside a basic block, a DAG, which we met in lesson 16, makes local optimization systematic. Process the instructions in order; for x = y op z, look for an existing node with operator op and children y and z. If one exists, the expression is common: just attach x to that node. Otherwise create a new node. Each node keeps a list of variables currently holding its value. When the DAG is built, regenerate code from it, computing each node once.

A DAG worked example: Take the block a = b + c; b = a - d; c = b + c; d = a - d. The first instruction creates a node for b + c, labelled a. The second creates a node for a - d, labelled b. The third needs b + c, but b now refers to the new node, not the original b, so this is a different expression: a new node b + c, labelled c. The fourth needs a - d with the same a and d as before, so it finds the node labelled b and attaches d to it. The DAG has three operation nodes instead of four. If b is not live on exit, the regenerated code is a = b + c; d = a - d; c = d + c.

Algebraic identities and reassociation: The DAG builder can also apply identities: x + 0 and x * 1 become x, x * 2 can become x + x, and commutativity means b + c and c + b share a node. Compilers must be careful with reassociation of floating point: in floating point arithmetic, ( a + b ) + c is not always equal to a + ( b + c ) because of rounding, so compilers do not reorder floating point sums unless the programmer allows it with a flag like -ffast-math.

Pitfalls with pointers and arrays: In the DAG, an assignment to an array element a [ j ] = y might change a [ i ] if i equals j, which the compiler often cannot know. So after such an assignment, any node reading from array a must be killed, meaning it cannot be reused. Pointers are worse: an assignment through *p might change any variable that p could point to. Alias analysis tries to prove which pointers cannot point to the same place, allowing more optimization.

Real life example 1, image filters on phones: A photo app applying a filter to a 12-megapixel image runs its inner loop 12 million times. Code motion moves constant brightness factors out of the loop, strength reduction turns pixel-address multiplications into additions, and CSE removes repeated address calculations for red, green and blue channels. The same filter, compiled with optimizations on, can run several times faster than with them off.

Real life example 2, debug vs release builds: A team in Dhaka building a Flutter app notices that their release build is much faster than their debug build. In the release build, the Dart compiler runs optimizations like inlining, constant folding, and dead code elimination, including removing debug-only checks guarded by constant flags. Debug builds keep the code close to the source so that breakpoints and step-by-step debugging work correctly.

Common mistakes: Treating two expressions as common when an operand was redefined between them. Moving a computation out of a loop when its operand changes inside the loop. Deleting a statement as dead when it has side effects. Forgetting to kill array or pointer nodes in a DAG after a store. Reordering floating point sums as if they were integers. Applying induction variable elimination without updating the loop test.

What exams ask: Explain the principal sources of optimization: CSE, copy propagation, dead code elimination, constant folding, code motion, induction variables and strength reduction, each with an example. Construct the DAG for a basic block and regenerate optimized code. Show the loop of a given code fragment before and after code motion, strength reduction and induction variable elimination. Distinguish local, global and interprocedural optimization.

Recap: Optimization transforms programs to run better without changing their meaning. Local techniques work within a block, often using a DAG; global techniques use data-flow analysis across the flow graph. Key transformations are common subexpression elimination, copy propagation, constant folding and propagation, and dead code elimination. Loop optimizations, code motion, induction variable elimination and strength reduction, give the biggest wins. Arrays, pointers and floating point require care. Next lesson we learn data-flow analysis, the machinery that makes global optimization safe, and wrap up the course.
key_points: An optimization must preserve meaning for every input; machine-independent ones work on IR.
Local optimization works within a basic block; global uses data-flow analysis over the flow graph; interprocedural crosses function calls.
CSE reuses an earlier result when operands are unchanged; copy propagation replaces x by y after x = y, often making the copy dead.
Constant folding evaluates constant expressions at compile time; constant propagation substitutes known constant values.
Code motion moves loop-invariant computations, like limit - 2, to the preheader.
Strength reduction replaces t1 = 4 * i in a loop with t1 = t1 + 4; induction variable elimination can remove i entirely.
DAG for a = b + c; b = a - d; c = b + c; d = a - d gives three operation nodes; with b dead: a = b + c; d = a - d; c = d + c.
lessons.tip: When building a DAG, keep a small table of which node each variable currently labels. Before reusing a node, check that its children are still the current nodes of those variables, not older versions.
lessons.task: Optimize: i = 1; L: t1 = 4 * i; t2 = a [ t1 ]; t3 = 4 * i; t4 = b [ t3 ]; t5 = t2 * t4; p = p + t5; i = i + 1; if i <= 20 goto L. Apply CSE, strength reduction and induction variable elimination, and write the final loop.

quiz.q: In t1 = 4 * i; t2 = a[t1]; t3 = 4 * i, when can t3 reuse t1?
options: When i has not been changed between the two computations
Only if a is a constant
quiz.explain: A common subexpression requires unchanged operands since the first computation.

quiz.q: Moving limit - 2 out of while (i <= limit - 2) is called:
quiz.explain: A loop-invariant computation is moved to the preheader.

quiz.q: Replacing t1 = 4 * i in a loop with t1 = t1 + 4 is:
quiz.explain: A multiplication becomes a cheaper addition each iteration.

quiz.q: Why do compilers usually not reassociate floating point additions?
options: It is illegal in C syntax
Rounding makes (a + b) + c differ from a + (b + c) in general
Floating point has no addition instruction
quiz.explain: Floating point addition is not associative because of rounding.

quiz.q: In the DAG for a = b + c; b = a - d; c = b + c; d = a - d, why is c = b + c not common with a = b + c?
options: Because c is on the left
Because b was redefined in between
quiz.explain: b now labels the a - d node, so b + c uses a different operand.

lessons.title: Data-Flow Analysis and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
Imagine the river network of Bangladesh during the monsoon. Rain falls in the hills, water flows down through rivers that split and join, and at every town an engineer wants to know which upstream sources reach that point. To find out, they do not follow every single drop; they write simple rules: what flows out of a town is what flowed in, minus what the dam blocks, plus what local rain adds. Applying these rules repeatedly across the map gives the answer for every town. Data-flow analysis does the same for programs: facts flow through the flow graph, and simple equations tell the compiler what is true at every point.

Why we need it: Global optimizations ask questions about the whole function. Is this x still holding the constant 10 here, on every path? Is the value computed in this statement ever used again? Has 4 * i already been computed on every path to this point? The answers depend on all possible paths through the flow graph, including loops that may run any number of times. Data-flow analysis computes safe answers for all program points at once, using sets and equations instead of simulating executions.

The framework: For each basic block B, we define in[B], the facts true at its start, and out[B], the facts true at its end. A transfer function describes how B changes the facts: usually out[B] = gen[B] ∪ ( in[B] − kill[B] ), where gen are facts B creates and kill are facts B destroys. A meet operation combines facts from several paths where they join: union if a fact needs to hold on some path, intersection if it must hold on every path. Analyses run forwards, following control flow, or backwards, against it.

Reaching definitions: A definition is a statement that assigns a value to a variable, such as d1: i = 0. Definition d reaches a point p if there is a path from d to p along which the variable is not redefined. This is a forward analysis with union: out[B] = gen[B] ∪ ( in[B] − kill[B] ), and in[B] is the union of out[P] over all predecessors P. gen[B] holds definitions in B that reach its end; kill[B] holds all other definitions of the same variables elsewhere in the program. Reaching definitions supports constant propagation and finding uses of uninitialised variables.

A reaching definitions example: B1 has d1: i = 0 and d2: s = 0. B2, a loop, has d3: s = s + i and d4: i = i + 1, then if i < n goto B2. B3 prints s. So gen[B1] = {d1, d2}, kill[B1] = {d3, d4}; gen[B2] = {d3, d4}, kill[B2] = {d1, d2}. Start with all out sets empty. Pass 1: out[B1] = {d1, d2}; in[B2] = out[B1] ∪ out[B2] = {d1, d2}; out[B2] = {d3, d4}. Pass 2: in[B2] = {d1, d2, d3, d4}; out[B2] stays {d3, d4}; in[B3] = {d3, d4}. Pass 3 changes nothing, so we stop. At the start of B2 both definitions of i reach, so i is not a constant there.

Live variable analysis: A variable is live at a point if its value may be used on some path from that point before being redefined. This is a backward analysis with union: in[B] = use[B] ∪ ( out[B] − def[B] ), and out[B] is the union of in[S] over all successors S. use[B] holds variables read in B before any assignment in B; def[B] holds variables assigned in B before any use in B. Liveness drives register allocation, through the interference graph of lesson 23, and dead code elimination: an assignment to a variable that is not live afterwards is dead.

Available expressions: An expression like x + y is available at a point if, on every path from the entry to that point, it has been computed and neither x nor y has been reassigned since. This is a forward analysis with intersection, because it must hold on all paths: in[B] is the intersection of out[P] over all predecessors. e_gen[B] holds expressions computed in B and not later killed in B; e_kill[B] holds expressions using a variable assigned in B. Global common subexpression elimination uses it: if x + y is available, the earlier result can be reused.

The iterative algorithm: All these analyses are solved the same way. Initialise every set: for union problems usually to empty, and for intersection problems like available expressions, every block except the entry starts with the set of all expressions. Then repeatedly recompute in and out for every block using the equations, until a full pass makes no change. Because sets can only grow for union problems, or only shrink for intersection problems, and there are finitely many facts, the algorithm always terminates. Visiting blocks in a good order, reverse postorder for forward problems, makes it converge in few passes.

Safety and conservativeness: Data-flow analysis may say a definition might reach or a variable might be live even when, in every real run, it never happens, because it assumes every path in the flow graph can be taken. That is acceptable: the answers are conservative, which means they may miss an optimization but never allow a wrong one. Saying a variable is live when it is not wastes a register; saying it is dead when it is live would break the program.

A live variables example: Use the same three blocks. B3 prints s, so use[B3] = {s} and in[B3] = {s}. B2 reads s and i before assigning them, and also reads n in the test, so use[B2] = {s, i, n} and def[B2] is empty, because each variable is used before it is assigned. out[B2] is the union of in[B2] and in[B3]. Starting from empty sets and working backwards: in[B2] = {s, i, n}, out[B2] = {s, i, n}. B1 assigns i and s before any use, so def[B1] = {i, s}, use[B1] is empty, and in[B1] = out[B1] − def[B1] = {n}. So only n must hold a meaningful value when the function starts, which is exactly right: n is the input.

Dominators: In a flow graph, node d dominates node n if every path from the entry to n goes through d. Every node dominates itself, and the entry dominates every node. Dominators can be computed as a data-flow problem with intersection: D(n) = {n} ∪ the intersection of D(p) over all predecessors p. Dominators are drawn as a dominator tree, where each node's parent is its immediate dominator. They are central to finding loops and to building SSA form.

Natural loops: An edge n to h is a back edge if h dominates n. The natural loop of a back edge is h together with all nodes that can reach n without going through h; h is the loop header, the single entry. In the array-sum example of lesson 22, the edge from B3 back to B2 is a back edge because B2 dominates B3, and the natural loop is {B2, B3}. Loop optimizations like code motion work on natural loops, placing hoisted code in a preheader just before the header.

Putting the course together: You have now seen the whole journey. The lexer turns characters into tokens using regular expressions and DFAs. The parser builds structure using a context-free grammar, top-down with LL(1) or bottom-up with LR, SLR and LALR tables, often generated by Yacc or Bison. Syntax-directed translation, through SDDs and SDTs, builds syntax trees, checks types, and emits three-address code with backpatching for control flow. The run-time environment organises stacks, heaps and activation records. Optimization improves the IR using DAGs, loop transformations and data-flow analysis, and the code generator selects instructions, allocates registers by graph colouring, and polishes with peephole rules.

Just-in-time compilation: Not all compilers run before the program. A JIT compiler translates code while the program runs. The Java HotSpot virtual machine first interprets bytecode, watches which methods are hot, and compiles those to native code with heavy optimization. JavaScript engines like V8 in Chrome do something similar for web pages. JITs can optimize using information only available at run time, such as the actual types flowing through a function, and can undo an optimization if an assumption later turns out false.

GCC and LLVM: Two open source compiler families dominate today. GCC, the GNU Compiler Collection, was first released by Richard Stallman in 1987 and compiles C, C++, Fortran and more for a huge range of processors. LLVM began as a research project by Chris Lattner at the University of Illinois; it provides a reusable SSA-based IR and optimizer used by Clang for C and C++, by Swift, by Rust and by many other languages. Both follow the same architecture you studied: front end, IR, middle-end optimization passes, and back end.

Real life example 1, compiler warnings that save students: When you compile C code with warnings enabled, GCC or Clang may warn that a variable may be used uninitialised. That warning comes from data-flow analysis similar to reaching definitions: the compiler found a path from the entry to a use with no definition of the variable. Students preparing for programming contests in Bangladesh can avoid many wrong answers just by reading these warnings.

Real life example 2, apps on low-end phones: Many users in Bangladesh use affordable Android phones with limited memory and processing power. Optimizing compilers, the Android runtime and the Dart compiler behind Flutter apps use liveness for register allocation, available expressions for removing repeated work, and loop analysis for hoisting code. All of this helps the same app run smoothly and save battery on a cheaper device.

Common mistakes: Using intersection for reaching definitions or union for available expressions. Running live variable analysis forwards. Confusing use and def: a variable used and then assigned in a block is in use[B], not removed by def. Initialising available expressions to empty, which gives answers that are too small. Saying d dominates n when only some paths to n pass through d. Forgetting that the natural loop includes the header.

What exams ask: Define gen, kill, in and out and write the data-flow equations for reaching definitions, live variables and available expressions, stating direction and meet. Compute these sets for a given flow graph using the iterative algorithm. Define dominators, back edges and natural loops, and find them in a flow graph. Short notes on JIT compilation and on modern compiler infrastructures like GCC and LLVM. Explain how each analysis enables an optimization.

Recap: Data-flow analysis computes facts at every point of the flow graph using transfer functions and a meet operation. Reaching definitions is forward with union; live variables is backward with union; available expressions is forward with intersection. The iterative algorithm repeats until nothing changes, and its answers are conservative, so optimizations stay safe. Dominators and back edges reveal natural loops. With this, you have travelled the whole compiler, from characters to optimized machine code, and you are ready to read real compiler code and build your own small language.
key_points: Data-flow analysis uses in[B], out[B], a transfer function out = gen ∪ (in − kill), and a meet operation at joins.
Reaching definitions: forward, union over predecessors; supports constant propagation and uninitialised-use warnings.
Live variables: backward, in[B] = use[B] ∪ (out[B] − def[B]), out = union over successors; used for register allocation and dead code.
Available expressions: forward, intersection over predecessors; used for global common subexpression elimination.
The iterative algorithm repeats until no set changes; it terminates and gives conservative, safe answers.
d dominates n if every path from entry to n passes through d; a back edge n to h has h dominating n, and defines a natural loop.
JIT compilers like HotSpot and V8 compile at run time; GCC (1987, Stallman) and LLVM (Lattner) follow front end, IR, optimizer, back end.
lessons.tip: For any data-flow problem, first write down three things: direction (forward or backward), meet (union or intersection), and initial values. Most mistakes come from getting one of these wrong.
lessons.task: For the flow graph B1: a = 1; b = 2 → B2: c = a + b; if c > 10 goto B4 → B3: a = a + 1; goto B2 → B4: print c, compute reaching definitions and live variables for every block with the iterative algorithm, and identify the back edge and natural loop.

quiz.q: Which analysis is backward with union as its meet operation?
quiz.explain: Liveness looks at future uses, so it flows backwards, and one path with a use is enough.

quiz.q: Why does available expressions use intersection at join points?
options: Because it is a backward analysis
Because sets must shrink to zero
Because an expression must have been computed on every path
quiz.explain: Reuse is safe only if the value exists no matter which path was taken.

quiz.q: What does it mean that d dominates n?
options: Every path from the entry to n passes through d
d comes right before n in the code
d and n are in the same block
quiz.explain: Domination is about all paths from the entry.

quiz.q: Which equation is correct for reaching definitions?
options: in[B] = intersection of out[P] over predecessors
quiz.explain: Definitions generated in B, plus incoming ones not killed by B, reach the end of B.

quiz.q: Why do data-flow analyses give conservative answers?
options: They run on the target machine
They assume every path in the flow graph can be taken
quiz.explain: Considering all paths may include impossible ones, so answers are safe but sometimes imprecise.
